title: The off-diagonal low rank property: new opportunities for low-scaling computational chemistry methods
summary: Many matrices in computational chemistry are neither sparse nor low-rank, making the design of low-scaling algorithms difficult. In this Perspective, we point out that many important matrices in computational chemistry, such as the Coulomb matrix, the electronic repulsion integral tensor, the density matrix, the localized molecular orbital (LMO) coefficient matrix, the Fock matrix, and the nuclear Hessian matrix share the same property: when their basis functions are suitably ordered, their off-diagonal blocks have low numerical ranks (despite that they as a whole have high numerical ranks). This property, termed off-diagonal low rank (ODLR), has been extensively studied in the mathematics community, but has surprisingly found very little use in computational chemistry. This Perspective reviews the existing mathematical literature on how to use the ODLR property of matrices to compactly store, as well as efficiently calculate or use them. Subsequently, we review the use of the ODLR property in computational chemistry, and point out possible future opportunities of devising new low-scaling methods for dense, full-rank matrices, exploiting the ODLR property. In particular, we prove for the first time that Fock matrices and LMO coefficient matrices satisfy the ODLR property, even if the system is gapless (in which case the matrices are dense). This paves the way to linear scaling electronic structure calculations of gapless systems at zero electronic temperature.

AI.tldr: This Perspective reviews the off-diagonal low rank (ODLR) property of matrices in computational chemistry, which allows seemingly dense, full-rank matrices to be compactly stored and manipulated. The authors review existing mathematical literature on exploiting ODLR, survey its sparse use in chemistry, and prove for the first time that Fock matrices and localized molecular orbital coefficient matrices satisfy ODLR even for gapless systems, enabling linear-scaling electronic structure calculations at zero temperature.
AI.motivation: Many important matrices in computational chemistry are neither sparse nor low-rank, making low-scaling algorithms difficult. The authors point out that many of these matrices (Coulomb matrix, ERI tensor, density matrix, LMO coefficient matrix, Fock matrix, nuclear Hessian) share the ODLR property—their off-diagonal blocks have low numerical ranks when basis functions are suitably ordered—yet this property has seen very little use in computational chemistry despite extensive study in mathematics.
AI.method: The paper is a Perspective that (1) reviews the mathematical literature on exploiting ODLR for compact storage and efficient computation, (2) surveys existing applications of ODLR in computational chemistry, and (3) proves theoretically that Fock matrices and LMO coefficient matrices satisfy ODLR even for gapless (metallic) systems where the matrices are dense.
AI.result: The authors establish that ODLR is a common property across several key computational chemistry matrices. They provide the first proof that Fock matrices and LMO coefficient matrices satisfy ODLR even in gapless systems, a setting previously thought to preclude such structure and linear-scaling treatments.
AI.conclusion: Exploiting the ODLR property paves the way for new low-scaling (linear-scaling) electronic structure methods applicable to dense, full-rank matrices, including gapless systems at zero electronic temperature. The authors also highlight future opportunities for devising new algorithms based on this property.

title: Franson-Interferometric Bounds on Entangled Two-Photon Absorption
summary: Entangled photons offer quantum correlations with no classical analogue. In entangled pair two-photon absorption (ETPA), absorption rate is predicted to scale linearly rather than quadratically with photon flux, promising molecular excitation at fluxes far below the classical threshold. Reported ETPA cross sections nevertheless vary widely across experiments, largely since the observable, the differential of the transmitted flux or weak fluorescence, is difficult to separate from scattering and linear losses. We present a method which uses Franson interference to study entangled two-photon absorption through delay-dependent coincidence measurements on dye molecules. Applying the method to Rhodamine 6G, we observe a small asymmetry in the Franson interference envelope and obtain a model-derived effective cross section of approximately 2.1 E(-21) centimeter squared for Rhodamine 6G. However, the estimated systematic uncertainty does not allow a definitive ETPA assignment. Instead, the experiment establishes a quantitative bound on the ETPA response and provides a background-free benchmark for future measurements.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a method using Franson interference to study entangled two-photon absorption (ETPA) via delay-dependent coincidence measurements on dye molecules. Applying this to Rhodamine 6G, they observe a small asymmetry in the Franson interference envelope and derive an effective ETPA cross section of ~2.1 × 10⁻²¹ cm², but with systematic uncertainty too large for a definitive ETPA assignment. The experiment establishes a quantitative bound on ETPA response and serves as a background-free benchmark.
AI.motivation: Reported ETPA cross sections vary widely across experiments, largely because the observable (differential of transmitted flux or weak fluorescence) is difficult to separate from scattering and linear losses. A background-free method is needed to reliably quantify ETPA.
AI.method: The authors use Franson interference to probe entangled two-photon absorption through delay-dependent coincidence measurements on dye molecules, specifically Rhodamine 6G. The asymmetry in the Franson interference envelope is analyzed with a model to extract an effective ETPA cross section.
AI.result: A small asymmetry in the Franson interference envelope is observed for Rhodamine 6G, yielding a model-derived effective ETPA cross section of approximately 2.1 × 10⁻²¹ cm². However, the systematic uncertainty precludes a definitive ETPA assignment; instead, a quantitative upper bound on the ETPA response is established.
AI.conclusion: The method provides a background-free benchmark for future ETPA measurements, addressing the long-standing problem of inconsistent ETPA cross-section values in the literature. While not conclusively confirming ETPA in Rhodamine 6G, it establishes a rigorous quantitative constraint.

title: ElemCo.jl: A Julia package for electron-correlation methods
summary: We present ElemCo.jl, an open-source Julia package for molecular electronic structure and properties calculations with a particular emphasis on Coupled Cluster and Distinguishable Cluster methods. The package provides a high-level, macro-based user interface which makes routine calculations accessible to users with no prior Julia experience. A newly developed visualizer, JLmol, assists in the graphical preparation of ElemCo.jl input files and displays results such as molecular orbitals. ElemCo.jl offers restricted closed-shell and unrestricted variants of state-of-the-art electron-correlation methods such as FCI, MP2, CCSD(T) as well as EOM-CCSD and the DC methods DCSD and DC-CCSDT. In addition to traditional approaches, ElemCo.jl provides recently developed methods that are currently unique to the package. These include tensor-decomposed implementations of DCSD and DC-CCSDT (SVD-DCSD and SVD-DC-CCSDT) as well as two-determinant and fixed-reference CC and DC methods. For excited-state calculations, ElemCo.jl also offers EOM-DCSD, which is benchmarked in this work against CC3 on the QUEST3 benchmark set, alongside EOM-CCSD. Furthermore, both ground and excited states, including those of multireference character, can be treated using CIPHI - an efficient selected Configuration Interaction (CI) approach employing a CIPSI/Heat-Bath-CI-based algorithm. Users can directly invoke internal functions from the input file, enabling them to test and compose new methods without the need to modify ElemCo.jl's source code. Also, ElemCo.jl can be readily interfaced with external quantum chemistry codes through the Fcidump format, for example as the high-level solver for transcorrelated Hamiltonians, periodic embedded fragments, etc. We provide a detailed overview of ElemCo.jl's methodological repertoire and discuss its technical details and implementation, performance, interfaces, and usage.

AI.tldr: ElemCo.jl is an open-source Julia package for molecular electronic structure calculations, emphasizing Coupled Cluster and Distinguishable Cluster methods. It offers a wide range of methods (FCI, MP2, CCSD(T), EOM-CCSD, DCSD, DC-CCSDT, and unique tensor-decomposed variants), a visualizer (JLmol), a macro-based user interface, and external interfaces via Fcidump format.
AI.motivation: To provide a comprehensive, open-source electronic structure package in Julia that covers both traditional and recently developed electron-correlation methods, with particular emphasis on Coupled Cluster and Distinguishable Cluster approaches, while making these advanced methods accessible to users without Julia experience.
AI.method: ElemCo.jl implements restricted closed-shell and unrestricted variants of FCI, MP2, CCSD(T), EOM-CCSD, DCSD, and DC-CCSDT, along with unique tensor-decomposed implementations (SVD-DCSD, SVD-DC-CCSDT), two-determinant and fixed-reference CC/DC methods, EOM-DCSD, and CIPHI (a selected CI approach using CIPSI/Heat-Bath-CI). It uses a macro-based user interface, a JLmol visualizer, and supports external interfaces via Fcidump format.
AI.result: The package provides a benchmarked EOM-DCSD against CC3 on the QUEST3 benchmark set, alongside EOM-CCSD. It supports ground and excited states including multireference character, and allows users to test and compose new methods directly from the input file without modifying source code.
AI.conclusion: ElemCo.jl offers a versatile platform for molecular electronic structure research with a broad methodological repertoire, user-friendly interface, and flexible interfaces with external codes, making it a useful tool for both routine calculations and method development.

title: Real-Time Emergence of Charge-Transfer-to-Solvent States from Core Excitation
summary: Charge-transfer-to-solvent (CTTS) excitations provide a chemically central route to generating hydrated electrons and initiating redox chemistry in solution, yet the earliest stage of CTTS---the formation of the excited state itself---is usually treated as instantaneous. Here we present a time-domain perspective of how CTTS character builds up during core-level photoexcitation of an aqueous metal ion. Using time-dependent configuration interaction, we simulate the coherent evolution of a dense manifold of core-excited states and track the ultrafast flow of electronic charge from the initially localized site into solvent-supported final states. We find that the dynamics evolves from a few-state, oscillatory behavior to effectively irreversible delocalization, as the charge disperses among many coupled configurations, providing a microscopic mechanism for the early-time emergence of CTTS character. Our results offer a transparent real-time interpretation of what core-level spectroscopies and core-hole-clock-type measurements can probe in solutions, outlining experimental signatures for probing the build-up of CTTS states on the core-hole-lifetime timescale. Looking ahead, attosecond and sub-femtosecond X-ray pump--probe approaches at X-ray free-electron lasers provide a realistic route to directly time-resolve the core-excited CTTS wave packets in solution.

AI.tldr: This paper simulates the ultrafast build-up of charge-transfer-to-solvent (CTTS) character during core-level photoexcitation of an aqueous metal ion using time-dependent configuration interaction, showing how electronic charge flows from a localized site into solvent-supported states and identifying experimental signatures for probing this process on core-hole-lifetime timescales.
AI.motivation: The earliest stage of CTTS—the formation of the excited state itself—is typically treated as instantaneous, yet understanding how CTTS character builds up is chemically central to hydrated electron generation and redox chemistry. A time-domain perspective is needed to reveal the microscopic mechanism of this ultrafast process.
AI.method: Time-dependent configuration interaction (TDCI) simulations are used to model the coherent evolution of a dense manifold of core-excited states, tracking the ultrafast flow of electronic charge from the initially localized site into solvent-supported final states.
AI.result: The dynamics evolve from a few-state oscillatory regime to effectively irreversible delocalization as charge disperses among many coupled configurations, providing a microscopic mechanism for early-time CTTS emergence. The results offer real-time interpretations of core-level spectroscopies and core-hole-clock measurements, outlining experimental signatures on core-hole-lifetime timescales.
AI.conclusion: Attosecond and sub-femtosecond X-ray pump–probe approaches at X-ray free-electron lasers provide a realistic route to directly time-resolve core-excited CTTS wave packets in solution, enabling direct experimental verification of the predicted dynamics.

title: Automatic generation of exchange-correlation response kernels
summary: Computing density-functional response properties requires contracting derivatives of the exchange--correlation (xc) energy with perturbed densities on a grid. While the xc functional's derivatives have long been available to high orders from libraries such as Libxc, the surrounding contraction layer - the chain rule that combines them with the grid-based basis-function and density data into the total xc contribution - has instead been hand-derived and hand-coded in every program, for every functional family, spin case, and property. We present libxckernel, a library that automatically generates this layer by symbolic differentiation. The xc functional's ingredients are expressed as sesquilinear forms in the density matrix, so the xc energy can be differentiated to any order while the functional derivatives remain opaque. The basis functions and the orbital coefficients may both be complex. The chain rule then produces any xc matrix element: Fock matrices, orbital Hessians, and response terms of any order. Terms sharing a pattern are collapsed for efficiency. Extensible plugins emit the expressions as NumPy Einstein sums, compiled C kernels with C++/Fortran interfaces, or host-program specific source code. libxckernel is free and open-source software under the BSD-3-Clause license, enabling rapid implementation of functionality missing from many electronic structure programs. We demonstrate it by extending Psi4 with meta-generalized gradient approximation (mGGA) response kernels for orbital stability analysis and time-dependent density-functional theory (TD-DFT), GGA and mGGA analytic nuclear Hessians, and exact quadrature grid response, and by extending GPAW with mGGA and triplet TD-DFT kernels and gradient-corrected kernels for periodic dielectric response.

AI.tldr: libxckernel is a new open-source library that automatically generates the contraction layer between exchange-correlation (xc) functional derivatives and grid-based density data via symbolic differentiation. It expresses xc functional ingredients as sesquilinear forms in the density matrix, enabling differentiation to arbitrary order to produce Fock matrices, orbital Hessians, and response terms. The library emits code as NumPy Einstein sums, compiled C kernels, or host-program-specific source code, and was demonstrated by extending Psi4 and GPAW with mGGA response kernels, analytic nuclear Hessians, and TD-DFT capabilities.
AI.motivation: Currently, the contraction layer that combines xc functional derivatives with grid-based basis-function and density data must be hand-derived and hand-coded for every electronic structure program, functional family, spin case, and property. This is a tedious, error-prone, and labor-intensive process that impedes the implementation of higher-order response properties.
AI.method: The library represents xc functional ingredients as sesquilinear forms in the density matrix, allowing the xc energy to be symbolically differentiated to any order while keeping functional derivatives opaque. The chain rule generates any xc matrix element (Fock matrices, orbital Hessians, response terms) with support for complex basis functions and orbital coefficients. Terms with shared patterns are collapsed for efficiency, and extensible plugins emit expressions as NumPy Einstein sums, compiled C kernels with C++/Fortran interfaces, or host-program-specific code.
AI.result: The library extends Psi4 with mGGA response kernels for orbital stability analysis and TD-DFT, GGA and mGGA analytic nuclear Hessians, and exact quadrature grid response. It also extends GPAW with mGGA and triplet TD-DFT kernels and gradient-corrected kernels for periodic dielectric response, demonstrating broad applicability across different electronic structure frameworks.
AI.conclusion: libxckernel automates and generalizes the hand-coded contraction layer for xc response properties, dramatically simplifying and accelerating the implementation of advanced functionality in electronic structure programs. As free and open-source software under BSD-3-Clause, it enables rapid development of missing capabilities such as mGGA response kernels and higher-order analytic derivatives across multiple codebases.

title: Measuring the Sr$^+$ 5s$_{1/2}$ Landé $g$-factor Using Singlet-Triplet Oscillations in a Circular Rydberg State of Strontium
summary: Circular states of strontium are promising platforms for quantum technologies. They exhibit much longer lifetimes than laser-accessible Rydberg states and possess an optically active ionic core that can be manipulated with laser light. Here we trap circular states in optical tweezers by exploiting the dynamical polarizability of the ionic core. We measure the decay of the orbital component of a n=51 circular state and observe singlet-triplet spin oscillations arising from the interplay of vector light shifts induced by the optical tweezers, spin-orbit coupling associated with the Rydberg electron, and the difference in Landé $g$-factor between the ionic core and the Rydberg electrons. By observing the two electron spin dynamics, we measure the spin-orbit interaction and the correction $δg \sim$ 10^(-5) of the Landé $g$-factor of the Sr$^+$ 5s$_{1/2}$ ionic core electron with respect to that of a free electron. This provides a first high-precision measurement of $g_{\textrm{Sr}^+, 5s_{1/2}}$ = 2.002290(1).

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates trapping of circular Rydberg states of strontium in optical tweezers using the dynamical polarizability of the ionic core, and uses the observed vector light shifts and spin-orbit coupling to perform a high-precision measurement of the Landé g-factor of the Sr+ 5s1/2 ionic core electron, obtaining g = 2.002290(1).
AI.motivation: Circular Rydberg states of strontium offer long lifetimes and an optically active ionic core, making them promising for quantum technologies. However, trapping them in optical tweezers and understanding their spin dynamics is challenging, and there is a need for high-precision measurements of the ionic core's magnetic properties, particularly the Landé g-factor.
AI.method: The authors trap n=51 circular states in optical tweezers using the dynamical polarizability of the ionic core. They measure the decay of the orbital component and observe singlet-triplet spin oscillations driven by the interplay of vector light shifts from the optical tweezers, spin-orbit coupling of the Rydberg electron, and the difference in Landé g-factors between the ionic core and the Rydberg electron.
AI.result: By observing the two-electron spin dynamics, the authors measure the spin-orbit interaction and the correction δg ≈ 10^-5 of the Landé g-factor of the Sr+ 5s1/2 ionic core electron relative to a free electron, yielding g_Sr+,5s1/2 = 2.002290(1).
AI.conclusion: The work establishes circular Rydberg states in optical tweezers as a viable platform for quantum technologies and provides the first high-precision measurement of the g-factor of the Sr+ 5s1/2 ionic core electron, opening avenues for precision metrology and quantum information applications.

title: Statistics as a local phase: crystalline order and quench dynamics of emergent dimers in Ising gauge theories
summary: How does the Bose or Fermi statistics of microscopic particles survive when confinement binds them into emergent bosonic composites? We address this question in the strong-coupling limit of a $2+1$D $\mathbb{Z}_2$ lattice gauge theory, where charges are confined into tightly bound pairs that can be described by an effective dimer model. We find that the statistics of the underlying matter is encoded entirely in a single local hopping phase $\varphi$ -$0$ for bosons, $π$ for fermions- while interactions remain statistics-independent. Treating $\varphi$ as a continuous parameter that interpolates between the two, we map the ground-state phase diagram with the help of tensor-network methods. The angle $\varphi$ itself drives a transition between a dimer-superfluid and dimer charge density wave state, while the magnetic coupling binds neighboring dimers into resonating pairs, in competition with the inter-dimer repulsion. We identify a novel gapped phase in which dimer pairs crystallize into an ordered pattern of resonating plaquettes. Finally, we propose a quench protocol under which identical dimer configurations evolve in markedly different ways depending on the statistics of their constituents. This provides a dynamical probe of the internal structure of dimers, and detects ordered phases through real time signatures, within reach of simulators that natively realize bosonic degrees of freedom.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how Bose/Fermi statistics of microscopic particles manifest in emergent bosonic composite particles (dimers) within a strongly-coupled 2+1D Z₂ lattice gauge theory. The statistics is encoded in a single local hopping phase φ (0 for bosons, π for fermions), which drives a phase transition between dimer-superfluid and dimer charge density wave states. A novel gapped phase with crystallized resonating plaquettes is identified, and a quench protocol is proposed as a dynamical probe of dimer internal statistics.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to understand how the quantum statistics of underlying microscopic particles survives and is expressed when those particles are confined into emergent bosonic composites, specifically within a strongly-coupled lattice gauge theory framework.
AI.method: The study employs an effective dimer model description of tightly bound charge pairs in the strong-coupling limit of a 2+1D Z₂ lattice gauge theory. The statistics is parameterized by a continuous hopping phase φ interpolating between bosonic (φ=0) and fermionic (φ=π) cases. Tensor-network methods are used to map the ground-state phase diagram, and a quench protocol is proposed for dynamical probing.
AI.result: The phase diagram reveals that φ itself drives a transition between dimer-superfluid and dimer charge density wave states. The magnetic coupling competes with inter-dimer repulsion, leading to binding of neighboring dimers into resonating pairs. A novel gapped phase is identified where dimer pairs crystallize into an ordered pattern of resonating plaquettes. The proposed quench protocol yields markedly different real-time dynamics for identical dimer configurations depending on the constituent statistics.
AI.conclusion: The statistics of underlying matter survives in emergent dimers as a single local hopping phase, offering a clean characterization and a protocol to dynamically probe the internal structure and ordered phases of these composites, accessible to simulators with native bosonic degrees of freedom.

title: Dynamical phase selection controls compute scaling in looped transformers
summary: A looped transformer performs inference by iterating a weight-tied map, making its computation a dynamical process whose cost is set by the resulting inference dynamics. Here we show that networks with identical architecture and objective, trained to identical accuracy, nevertheless realize distinct dynamical phases depending strongly on initialization, and that the bifurcation defining each phase determines how test-time compute scales. The phases are distinguished by their bifurcation mechanisms, including a saddle-node fold and a Neimark-Sacker-type transition to bounded nonstationary motion. In the fold phase, a one-dimensional normal-form reduction predicts both the relaxation-time and spectral-gap amplitudes from local derivatives of the trained map, yielding the parameter-free relation $τ(\varepsilon)[1-λ_{\max}(-\varepsilon)]\toπ$. Composed with a regular distribution of problem difficulty, the same critical slowing down produces the workload-level tail $P(τ>N)\sim N^{-2}$. In the Neimark--Sacker phase, the fold scaling law disappears rather than merely changing its prefactor. Thus, test-time compute is not determined by architecture alone. It is governed by the dynamical phase of the solution found by training.

AI.tldr: Looped transformers trained to identical accuracy can exhibit different dynamical phases depending on initialization, and the bifurcation type defining each phase determines how test-time compute scales. A fold bifurcation yields a universal parameter-free scaling relation and a workload-level tail, while a Neimark-Sacker transition produces bounded nonstationary motion with no fold scaling law.
AI.motivation: To understand how test-time compute in iterated (looped) transformers depends not just on architecture but on the dynamical phase of the trained solution, revealing that initialization plays a decisive role in determining inference dynamics and compute scaling.
AI.method: Analyzes weight-tied recurrent inference through the lens of dynamical systems, identifying distinct bifurcation mechanisms (saddle-node fold vs. Neimark-Sacker) that define phases. Uses a one-dimensional normal-form reduction near the fold to link local derivatives of the trained map to relaxation time and spectral gap, yielding a parameter-free relation τ(ε)[1−λmax(−ε)]→π, and composes this with a regular difficulty distribution to derive a workload tail.
AI.result: Networks with identical architecture and objective, trained to identical accuracy, nonetheless realize distinct dynamical phases depending strongly on initialization. The fold phase obeys a universal parameter-free critical-slowing-down relation, leading to a workload-level tail P(τ>N)∼N−2, whereas in the Neimark–Sacker phase this fold scaling disappears entirely rather than merely changing prefactor.
AI.conclusion: Test-time compute is not determined by architecture alone; it is governed by the dynamical phase of the solution found by training, with initialization exerting strong influence over which phase (and hence which compute scaling law) emerges.

title: Exact pair density wave in topological moire flat bands and universal superfluid stiffness
summary: Pair-density waves (PDWs) are unconventional superconducting states beyond the BCS paradigm, but identifying them unambiguously in microscopic lattice models is generally challenging due to various competing orders. In particular, an exact realization of PDW in interacting models with topological bands remains elusive. Here we construct an interacting model on a twisted bilayer checkerboard lattice (TBCB) featuring topological flat bands, and rigorously show that an exact PDW ground state can be induced by quantum geometric nesting (QGN), owing to its momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry. We further prove that the superfluid stiffness of any nondegenerate QGN superconductor (including the PDW studied here and uniform superconductor) obeys the universal relation $D_s=2N_{\rm flat}ν(1-ν)m_{\rm pair}^{-1}$, where $N_{\rm flat}$, $ν$, and $m_{\rm pair}$ are the number of flat bands, flat band filling, and the two-particle effective mass, respectively. Our results reveal a rich interplay among PDW order, quantum geometry, and band topology.

AI.tldr: The paper constructs an interacting model on a twisted bilayer checkerboard lattice with topological flat bands, rigorously proving an exact pair-density wave (PDW) ground state can be induced by quantum geometric nesting (QGN) due to momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry. It further proves a universal relation for superfluid stiffness of nondegenerate QGN superconductors: D_s = 2N_flat·ν(1-ν)/m_pair, connecting PDW order, quantum geometry, and band topology.
AI.motivation: Pair-density waves are unconventional superconducting states beyond BCS theory, but identifying them unambiguously in microscopic lattice models is difficult due to competing orders. Moreover, no exact realization of PDW in interacting models with topological bands existed previously, motivating the search for a rigorous construction.
AI.method: The authors construct an interacting model on a twisted bilayer checkerboard lattice (TBCB) featuring topological flat bands. They exploit quantum geometric nesting (QGN) enabled by the momentum-space nonsymmorphic symmetry to rigorously establish an exact PDW ground state, and derive a universal formula for the superfluid stiffness of nondegenerate QGN superconductors.
AI.result: An exact PDW ground state is rigorously shown to exist in the TBCB model, induced by QGN. A universal relation D_s = 2N_flat·ν(1-ν)/m_pair is proven for any nondegenerate QGN superconductor, where N_flat is the number of flat bands, ν is the flat band filling, and m_pair is the two-particle effective mass.
AI.conclusion: The results reveal a rich interplay among PDW order, quantum geometry, and band topology, providing a rigorous framework for understanding and identifying pair-density waves in topological flat band systems.

title: When chemical potential continuity fails: kinetic interface models for hydrogen isotope transport
summary: Macroscopic hydrogen transport codes model material interfaces with local thermodynamic equilibrium (LTE), imposing continuity of chemical potential as a per-species constraint. Three assumptions hide in that condition: fast interfacial equilibration, a single exchange pathway between the two sides, and a carrier species known in advance on each side. The literature scrutinises the first, but the other two are the more consequential failures, and neither survives at a metal/molten-salt interface. We replace the constraint with reversible reaction channels at the interface that obey mass action, with detailed balance fixing each ratio of rate constants from the thermodynamic data that already parameterise LTE, and we implement the framework in festim. LTE is recovered as the fast-kinetics limit of a single channel, in both its Sieverts/Sieverts and its Sieverts/Henry form, so the framework generalises LTE and does not compete with it. A Damköhler number delimits validity within a channel, a branching ratio between channels. In a representative nickel/FLiBe system, hydrogen partitions kinetically between molecular and fluoride carriers. The apparent interfacial law then drifts between Sieverts and Henry with loading and salt redox state, and an LTE condition underestimates the steady permeating flux. The measured pressure exponent is set by the branching ratio, not by any fixed property of the salt; a redox sweep at fixed temperature should continuously shift it between 0.5 and 1. With two isotopes, two metal-side species feed five salt-side carriers, and a per-species LTE condition is ill-posed.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies that LTE-based interface conditions in macroscopic hydrogen transport codes make three hidden assumptions (fast equilibration, single exchange pathway, known carrier species), of which the latter two fail at metal/molten-salt interfaces. The authors replace the per-species chemical potential continuity constraint with reversible, mass-action reaction channels whose rate constants are fixed by detailed balance from LTE thermodynamic data, implemented in festim. LTE is recovered as the fast-kinetics single-channel limit, a Damköhler number delimits validity within a channel, and a branching ratio between channels. In a Ni/FLiBe system, hydrogen partitions kinetically between molecular and fluoride carriers, the apparent interfacial law drifts between Sieverts and Henry, LTE underestimates steady permeating flux, and the pressure exponent is set by the branching ratio rather than salt properties.
AI.motivation: LTE-based interfacial constraints in hydrogen transport codes impose chemical potential continuity per species, which embeds three assumptions. The first (fast equilibration) is well studied, but the other two—a single exchange pathway and an a priori known carrier species on each side—are more consequential and both fail at metal/molten-salt interfaces. The work aims to correct these failures and provide a framework that generalises, rather than competes with, LTE.
AI.method: The authors replace the per-species LTE constraint with reversible reaction channels at the interface that obey mass action, with each ratio of rate constants fixed by detailed balance from the thermodynamic data already used to parameterise LTE. The framework is implemented in the festim transport code. A Damköhler number delimits validity within a channel, and a branching ratio governs competition between channels.
AI.result: LTE is recovered as the fast-kinetics limit of a single channel, in both Sieverts/Sieverts and Sieverts/Henry form. In a nickel/FLiBe system, hydrogen partitions kinetically between molecular and fluoride carriers. The apparent interfacial law drifts between Sieverts and Henry with loading and salt redox state, and LTE underestimates the steady permeating flux. The measured pressure exponent is set by the branching ratio (not any fixed salt property), and a redox sweep at fixed temperature should continuously shift it between 0.5 and 1. For two isotopes, a per-species LTE condition is ill-posed.
AI.conclusion: The kinetic interfacial reaction-channel framework generalises LTE and resolves pathologies that per-species LTE constraints cannot handle at metal/molten-salt interfaces, such as multiple concurrent carrier species, isotope cases, and pressure-exponent dependence on branching rather than salt properties.

title: Split Coaxial Cable Medium for Tunable Artificial Dielectrics and Plasmas
summary: We introduce the Split Coaxial Cable Medium (SCCM), a mechanically tunable, capacitively loaded wire medium supporting artificial-dielectric and artificial-plasma Bloch regimes with high in-plane isotropy. Its unit cell comprises coaxial conductors interrupted by axial gaps. Relative axial displacement continuously varies their capacitive overlap and series capacitance while preserving the transverse lattice geometry and leaving the unit-cell inductance approximately unchanged. Equivalent RLC parameters are derived directly from the geometry and incorporated into complementary analytical models. A spatially dispersive local-field model predicts the Bloch dispersion and isofrequency contours, whereas a multilayer homogenization model provides the modal impedance, closed-form estimates of the low-frequency Bloch refractive index and plasma frequency, and loss-inclusive finite-slab scattering. Full-wave eigenmode and finite-slab simulations validate the predictions. Over the investigated displacement range, simulations yield tunabilities of $46\%$ in the low-frequency Bloch refractive index, from $n_{0,\min}=1.42$ to $n_{0,\max}=2.28$, and $21\%$ in the plasma frequency, from $f_{\mathrm{p},\min}=9.45~\mathrm{GHz}$ to $f_{\mathrm{p},\max}=11.61~\mathrm{GHz}$, while confirming high in-plane isotropy near the $Γ$ point in both regimes. These characteristics make the SCCM promising for gradient-index devices, directive antennas, and tunable plasma haloscopes.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the Split Coaxial Cable Medium (SCCM), a mechanically tunable wire medium composed of coaxial conductors with axial gaps whose capacitive coupling can be adjusted via relative axial displacement. The work derives equivalent RLC parameters from geometry, develops two complementary analytical models (a spatially dispersive local-field model and a multilayer homogenization model), and validates them with full-wave simulations. Tunabilities of 46% in the low-frequency Bloch refractive index and 21% in plasma frequency are demonstrated, with high in-plane isotropy preserved. Applications include gradient-index devices, directive antennas, and tunable plasma haloscopes.
AI.motivation: To create a mechanically tunable version of capacitively loaded wire media that maintains high in-plane isotropy while allowing continuous, large-range tuning of its artificial-dielectric and artificial-plasma properties, without altering the transverse lattice geometry.
AI.method: The unit cell consists of coaxial conductors interrupted by axial gaps; relative axial displacement varies capacitive overlap and series capacitance while keeping inductance approximately constant. Equivalent RLC parameters are derived geometrically. Two complementary analytical models are used: (1) a spatially dispersive local-field model for Bloch dispersion and isofrequency contours, and (2) a multilayer homogenization model for modal impedance, closed-form low-frequency Bloch refractive index, plasma frequency, and loss-inclusive finite-slab scattering. Full-wave eigenmode and finite-slab simulations validate the predictions.
AI.result: Over the investigated displacement range, simulations show a 46% tunability in the low-frequency Bloch refractive index (n0 from 1.42 to 2.28) and 21% tunability in the plasma frequency (fp from 9.45 GHz to 11.61 GHz), while confirming high in-plane isotropy near the Γ point in both artificial-dielectric and artificial-plasma regimes.
AI.conclusion: The SCCM is a promising platform for mechanically tunable electromagnetic metamaterials, with potential applications in gradient-index devices, directive antennas, and tunable plasma haloscopes.

title: Critical Properties and Glass Transitions in Randomly Coupled Fields
comment: Main text: 5 pages. Supplemental Material: 20 pages
summary: We study an assembly of $N$ scalar fields coupled via a quenched random interaction, equivalent to a spin glass whose spins are promoted to $d$-dimensional fields. When $N$ is large, the random coupling matrix produces a family of Gaussian universality classes whose critical exponents are determined by the behavior of the eigenvalue density near the spectral edge. For a Wigner matrix, the correlation length diverges at criticality but the susceptibility remains finite, and one-loop replica analysis supports an upper critical dimension of unity. In an exactly solvable spherical variant, the heat capacity jumps at the transition in $d>1$, and correlations remain pinned to their critical form throughout the glass phase, giving generic scale invariance despite the absence of a Goldstone mode.

It identifies Gaussian universality classes governed by the eigenvalue density near the spectral edge, finding diverging correlation length but finite susceptibility for Wigner matrices, an upper critical dimension of unity, and exact spherical solutions showing a heat capacity jump in d>1 with critical correlations pinned throughout the glass phase producing generic scale invariance without a Goldstone mode.
AI.motivation: To understand the critical behavior and universality of a field-theoretic generalization of spin glasses, where spins are promoted to d-dimensional fields coupled by quenched random interactions, and to characterize the nature of the glass transition and scaling properties in this setting.
AI.method: The paper employs large-N random matrix theory to classify universality classes via eigenvalue density behavior near the spectral edge, combined with one-loop replica analysis to determine critical exponents and upper critical dimension, alongside an exactly solvable spherical variant to access exact thermodynamic properties.
AI.result: For Wigner-type random coupling matrices, the correlation length diverges at criticality while susceptibility remains finite; one-loop replica analysis gives an upper critical dimension of unity (dc=1). In the exactly solvable spherical variant, the heat capacity exhibits a jump at the transition in d>1, and correlations remain pinned to their critical form throughout the glass phase, yielding generic scale invariance despite no Goldstone mode being present.
AI.conclusion: The random-field spin glass model exhibits Gaussian universality classes tied to spectral-edge properties of the coupling matrix. The spherical case reveals non-standard critical phenomena: a discontinuous heat capacity in d>1 and critical-like correlations persisting in the glass phase, implying generic scale invariance arises without a broken continuous symmetry or Goldstone mode.

title: Quantized Transport through a Supermoiré Chern Mosaic
summary: Magic-angle helical trilayer graphene---three graphene layers sequentially twisted in the same direction by $\sim1.8^\circ$---relaxes into a mosaic of domains that, at zero field, carry opposite valley-resolved Chern numbers, with boundaries hosting a network of gapless conducting modes. Charge transport through this network depends sensitively on how the modes connect and scatter, making well-quantized transport unlikely. Contrary to this expectation, we observe a field-induced Chern gap with Chern number $C=-6$ emanating from charge neutrality; in this gap, the Hall resistance is quantized to within $2\%$ of the expected value, $-h/6e^2$, at 4.6 K. We explain this behavior using both Hofstadter and orbital Zeeman calculations, which show that a moderate magnetic field drives a valley-selective topological transition. Above the transition, the total Chern number of the occupied states in each spin-valley flavor becomes identical across neighboring domains, and the domain-wall modes can become gapped. Though the central valence-band Chern numbers still differ between the two domain types, the observed quantized transport attests to a global gap.

AI.tldr: Magic-angle helical trilayer graphene, despite its mosaic of domains with opposite valley-resolved Chern numbers, exhibits a field-induced Chern gap with C=-6 and Hall resistance quantized to within 2% at 4.6 K. This is explained by a valley-selective topological transition driven by moderate magnetic fields, where neighboring domains acquire identical total Chern numbers and domain-wall modes become gapped.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether the complex domain network in magic-angle helical trilayer graphene permits quantized transport, which was expected to be unlikely due to the mosaic of domains with opposite valley-resolved Chern numbers and gapless domain-wall conducting modes.
AI.method: Experimental transport measurements combined with theoretical Hofstadter and orbital Zeeman calculations to explain the observed quantum Hall effect.
AI.result: A field-induced Chern gap with C=-6 is observed at charge neutrality, with Hall resistance quantized to -h/6e^2 within 2% at 4.6 K. The calculations show a moderate magnetic field drives a valley-selective topological transition, making the total Chern number of occupied states in each spin-valley flavor identical across neighboring domains, allowing domain-wall modes to become gapped.
AI.conclusion: Despite differing central valence-band Chern numbers between domain types, a global gap is formed and quantized transport is achieved, demonstrating that topological transitions under magnetic field can reconcile the domain network into a globally coherent quantum Hall state.

title: Beyond-EUV spectrum of highly-charged gadolinium
summary: We report ab initio relativistic calculations on the complex Gd$^{18+}$ and Gd$^{26+}$ highly-charged ions, which are relevant to beyond-extreme-ultraviolet (BEUV) light sources based on laser-produced gadolinium plasmas. Using the particle-hole configuration-interaction with many-body perturbation theory (CI+MBPT) method, we systematically saturate the $n=4$ configuration space and determine the influence of multiply-excited states on the emissivity spectrum. For Gd$^{26+}$ we find behavior analogous to that of its isoelectronic counterpart Sn$^{12+}$, with strong contributions from multiply-excited states and a significant appearance of even quadruply-excited states at certain effective temperatures. In contrast, the industry-relevant 6.7\,nm emission of Pd-like Gd$^{18+}$ is dominated by the singly excited $4d^{10}$ $^{1}S_{0}$ - $4d^{9}4f$ $^{1}P_{1}$ transition, while multiply-excited states primarily contribute to out-of-band emission.

AI.tldr: Ab initio relativistic CI+MBPT calculations on Gd$^{18+}$ and Gd$^{26+}$ highly-charged ions reveal that multiply-excited states significantly impact EUV emissivity spectra, with Gd$^{26+}$ showing behavior analogous to Sn$^{12+}$ including quadruply-excited contributions, while the 6.7 nm emission of Pd-like Gd$^{18+}$ is dominated by a single $4d^{10}$ $^{1}S_{0}$ - $4d^{9}4f$ $^{1}P_{1}$ transition with multiply-excited states contributing mainly out-of-band.
AI.motivation: To understand the emissivity spectra of gadolinium highly-charged ions relevant to beyond-extreme-ultraviolet (BEUV) light sources based on laser-produced gadolinium plasmas, specifically to determine how multiply-excited states influence emission in the 6.7 nm spectral region.
AI.method: Particle-hole configuration-interaction with many-body perturbation theory (CI+MBPT) calculations at the ab initio relativistic level, systematically saturating the n=4 configuration space to assess multiply-excited state contributions.
AI.result: For Gd$^{26+}$, strong contributions from multiply-excited states (including even quadruply-excited states at certain temperatures) were found, analogous to its isoelectronic counterpart Sn$^{12+}$. For Gd$^{18+}$, the 6.7 nm emission is dominated by the singly excited $4d^{10}$ $^{1}S_{0}$ - $4d^{9}4f$ $^{1}P_{1}$ transition, while multiply-excited states mainly contribute to out-of-band emission.
AI.conclusion: The two gadolinium ions exhibit fundamentally different spectral character: Gd$^{26+}$ relies heavily on multiply-excited state contributions (analogous to Sn$^{12+}$), whereas Pd-like Gd$^{18+}$'s key 6.7 nm emission arises from a single dominant transition, with multiply-excited states contributing predominantly off-band.

title: Time and Momentum Resolved Tunneling Spectroscopy of Floquet dynamics
summary: Periodically driven quantum systems provide a powerful route to engineer novel states of matter by controlling their effective Hamiltonians through external fields. However, most treatments are usually simplified by considering the high-frequency limit, and do not account for the processes taking place in the transient regime during the onset of the drive. In this work, we introduce a time and momentum resolved tunneling spectroscopy protocol to probe the instantaneous energy spectrum of Floquet-driven systems beyond the high-frequency regime, capturing both emergent effects and non-adiabatic phenomena without requiring explicit reconstruction of the full time-dependent Green's function. We benchmark the method on driven non-interacting fermionic models, and then generalize the approach to strongly correlated systems with the aid of time-dependent density matrix renormalization group techniques. We also provide a microscopic description to the emergence of in-gap states under resonant driving, and briefly explore its finite temperature analog.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a time- and momentum-resolved tunneling spectroscopy protocol to probe the instantaneous energy spectrum of Floquet-driven quantum systems beyond the high-frequency regime, capturing emergent and non-adiabatic effects without needing full time-dependent Green's function reconstruction. The method is benchmarked on driven non-interacting fermionic models and extended to strongly correlated systems via time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (tDMRG) techniques, with a microscopic description of in-gap states under resonant driving and a finite-temperature analog.
AI.motivation: Most treatments of periodically driven quantum systems are oversimplified by assuming the high-frequency limit and neglect transient-regime processes during the onset of the drive. A method is needed to probe the instantaneous energy spectrum beyond this limit.
AI.method: Introduction of a time- and momentum-resolved tunneling spectroscopy protocol that probes the instantaneous energy spectrum of Floquet-driven systems without explicit full reconstruction of the time-dependent Green's function. The method is benchmarked on driven non-interacting fermionic models and generalized to strongly correlated systems using time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (tDMRG) techniques.
AI.result: The protocol successfully captures both emergent effects and non-adiabatic phenomena in Floquet-driven systems beyond the high-frequency regime. It provides a microscopic description of in-gap states emerging under resonant driving and explores a finite-temperature analog.
AI.conclusion: The proposed tunneling spectroscopy approach offers a practical and efficient means to probe Floquet-driven spectra in real time, applicable to both non-interacting and strongly correlated quantum systems, and sheds light on the microscopic origin of in-gap states under resonant driving.

title: Neural Renormalization Group Flow for Percolation
summary: Machine learning offers a possible route to data-driven real-space renormalization when the relevant observables are nonlocal and difficult to prescribe explicitly. We explore this idea for two-dimensional site percolation developping a supervised, scale-shared neural architecture. The model recursively applies the same learned coarse-graining rule across scales, producing a latent field from which the crossing probability is predicted, while a corresponding fine-graining decoder reconstructs the largest-cluster mask. Trained only on small lattices, the model extrapolates to substantially larger systems, recovers the spanning cluster with high fidelity, and produces observables obeying the expected finite-size scaling near the critical point. We observe that to get such performance it is key that the learned latent representation exhibits critical fluctuations and scale-dependent flows consistent with the renormalization-group structure of percolation.

AI.tldr: A supervised, scale-shared neural architecture applies a learned coarse-graining rule recursively to perform data-driven real-space renormalization for 2D site percolation, predicting crossing probabilities and reconstructing the spanning cluster. Trained on small lattices, it extrapolates to larger systems and produces observables with correct finite-size scaling near criticality.
AI.motivation: Machine learning offers a route to data-driven real-space renormalization when relevant observables are nonlocal and difficult to prescribe explicitly, as in percolation where the crossing probability and cluster structure involve nonlocal information.
AI.method: A supervised, scale-shared neural architecture is developed that recursively applies the same learned coarse-graining rule across scales. It produces a latent field used to predict the crossing probability, while a fine-graining decoder reconstructs the largest-cluster mask. Training is performed only on small lattices.
AI.result: The model extrapolates to substantially larger systems, recovers the spanning cluster with high fidelity, and produces observables obeying the expected finite-size scaling near the critical point. Performance depends critically on the learned latent representation exhibiting critical fluctuations and scale-dependent flows consistent with the renormalization-group structure of percolation.
AI.conclusion: A scale-shared neural coarse-graining approach can effectively learn the renormalization-group structure of percolation from small-system data alone, enabling accurate prediction of nonlocal observables and cluster reconstruction on much larger systems, provided the latent representation faithfully reproduces critical fluctuations and RG flow.

title: Supercurrent detection and manipulation of topological phase transitions in Shiba-Majorana hybrid systems
summary: The non-Abelian statistics of Majorana zero modes has inspired numerous proposals for their detection and manipulation in topological superconductors. Implementations based on magnetic adatoms deposited on superconductors draw particular attention due to their capabilities for precise atomic manipulation and the control over disorder. Here, we propose a scheme for detecting changes in the ground state parity of a topologically non-trivial adatom system by passing supercurrent through their low-energy modes. We unravel characteristic discontinuities in the critical current driven by zero-energy level crossings. We apply these findings to a setup where the Majorana coupling is mediated by a single control magnetic adatom hosting a Yu-Shiba-Rusinov state, and test the robustness of our results against finite temperatures and different tunneling regimes. Our findings introduce a non-invasive approach for reading out and controlling the ground state parity of Majorana states in Shiba-Majorana hybrid systems.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a non-invasive scheme to detect changes in ground state parity of Majorana zero modes in magnetic adatom systems on superconductors by passing supercurrent through their low-energy modes, revealing characteristic discontinuities in critical current driven by zero-energy level crossings.
AI.motivation: Non-Abelian statistics of Majorana zero modes motivates detection schemes, and magnetic adatom implementations offer precise atomic control. The goal is to find a non-invasive readout method for ground state parity in Shiba-Majorana hybrid systems.
AI.method: The authors propose passing supercurrent through the low-energy modes of a topologically non-trivial adatom system and analyzing discontinuities in the critical current arising from zero-energy level crossings. They apply this to a setup where Majorana coupling is mediated by a single control magnetic adatom hosting a Yu-Shiba-Rusinov state, and test robustness against finite temperatures and different tunneling regimes.
AI.result: Characteristic discontinuities in the critical current are found to be driven by zero-energy level crossings, providing a detectable signature of ground state parity changes. The results remain robust at finite temperatures and across different tunneling regimes.
AI.conclusion: The findings introduce a non-invasive approach for reading out and controlling ground state parity of Majorana states in Shiba-Majorana hybrid systems.

title: Milled to order: toward predictive mechanochemistry of halide perovskites
summary: Mechanochemical milling is regarded as a scalable, solvent-free method that makes halide perovskites that solution processing cannot. Its deeper promise, though, is that mechanical force could become a new axis of synthetic control to turn milling from an empirical method into a predictive science. Halide perovskites are the ideal platform to establish this: their soft lattices and low formation energies make them intrinsically responsive to mechanical activation. Realising this requires settling what milling actually makes, and how: can a milled phase genuinely be trapped outside equilibrium, or is it just a convenient way to the equilibrium phase, and by what atomistic pathway does it work? These questions are mostly answered by assumption, while the in-situ and computational tools that resolved them for other material classes already exist. Closing this gap will unlock two design capabilities: mechanical energy used as a synthetic variable to tune phase selection, and metastability made programmable, producing trapped phases, specific intermediates, and compositions that have no possible solution route. Finally, two tests decide whether that control reaches practice: the state engineered during milling must survive into a working device, and the method must prove genuinely greener across the full device life cycle, rather than just solvent-free.

AI.tldr: This perspective argues that mechanochemical milling of halide perovskites could evolve from an empirical method into a predictive synthetic science by using mechanical force as a controlled axis for phase selection and programmable metastability, but this requires resolving fundamental questions about what milling actually produces and by what atomistic pathway, using in-situ and computational tools that already exist for other material classes.
AI.motivation: Mechanochemical milling is currently an empirical, scalable, solvent-free method for making halide perovskites, but its deeper potential—using mechanical force as a controllable synthetic variable to trap non-equilibrium phases—remains unrealized because key questions about the actual products and atomistic mechanisms of milling are largely answered by assumption rather than evidence.
AI.method: The paper proposes closing the knowledge gap by applying existing in-situ characterization and computational tools (already used for other material classes) to mechanochemical milling of halide perovskites. It outlines three guiding questions: (1) what phase milling actually produces, (2) whether milled phases can be genuinely trapped outside equilibrium versus merely fast routes to equilibrium, and (3) what atomistic pathway milling proceeds through.
AI.result: The paper identifies two design capabilities that would result from closing this gap: (a) using mechanical energy as a synthetic variable to tune phase selection, and (b) making metastability programmable to produce trapped phases, specific intermediates, and compositions inaccessible by solution processing.
AI.conclusion: Two practical tests will determine whether this control translates to real-world application: the milled state must survive through fabrication into a working device, and the method must prove genuinely greener across the entire device life cycle—not merely solvent-free in the synthesis step.

title: Ternary-Valued Finite-Difference Time-Domain Method: Equivalence with the Yee Scheme Through Noise-Shaped Quantisation
summary: Motivated by the rapid development of quantised large language models, which substantially reduce computational cost and enable efficient artificial intelligence on resource-constrained and consumer hardware, I demonstrate that finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) dynamics can be reproduced with field variables restricted to the ternary alphabet ${-1,0,+1}$. The resulting update requires no run-time multiplication or floating-point arithmetic and represents each field component with just $\log_2 3\simeq1.58$ bits. A true state accumulator performs the integration, while a second-order noise-shaped encoder with an independent error register performs the quantisation. The Courant number S serves simultaneously as an exact fixed-point ratio and as the encoder's oversampling ratio. Ternary FDTD converges to the standard Yee scheme in the small-S limit while substantially reducing state storage and arithmetic complexity. Its extension to acoustics, Virieux-type elastodynamics and Schrodinger-equation solvers points to a broader class of quantised physics solvers for resource-constrained and specialised hardware.

AI.tldr: The paper demonstrates that finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations can be executed using only ternary field values {-1,0,+1}, eliminating runtime multiplication and floating-point arithmetic. Each field component uses just ~1.58 bits. A state accumulator handles integration while a second-order noise-shaping encoder with an independent error register performs quantization, with the Courant number serving as both a fixed-point ratio and the encoder's oversampling ratio. Ternary FDTD converges to the standard Yee scheme as the Courant number approaches zero, reducing storage and computational complexity, and extends to acoustics, elastodynamics, and Schrödinger-equation solvers.
AI.motivation: The rapid development of quantised large language models has demonstrated substantial computational cost reductions and enabled efficient AI on resource-constrained hardware. This motivates exploring similar quantization strategies for physics solvers, specifically FDTD, to enable efficient numerical simulation on specialized and low-resource hardware.
AI.method: The approach restricts all field variables to a ternary alphabet {-1,0,+1}, eliminating runtime multiplication and floating-point operations. Integration is performed via a true state accumulator, while quantization is handled by a second-order noise-shaped encoder with a separate error register. The Courant number S acts as both the exact fixed-point ratio and the encoder's oversampling ratio, coupling numerical stability with quantization performance.
AI.result: Ternary FDTD converges to the standard Yee scheme in the small-S limit while substantially reducing state storage (each field component uses only log2(3) ≈ 1.58 bits) and arithmetic complexity. The approach also extends successfully to acoustics, Virieux-type elastodynamics, and Schrödinger-equation solvers.
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a broader class of quantised physics solvers for resource-constrained and specialised hardware, analogous to the success of quantization in large language models. Ternary FDTD offers a viable path to extremely low-precision numerical simulation without sacrificing convergence to standard results.

title: Information-theoretic formulation of the Traveling Salesman Problem
summary: The Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP) asks for the shortest route to visit a set of cities exactly once. It combines a simple local rule - each city must be visited once - with a hard, global constraint- all cities must be traversed within a single cycle. We cast the problem within a probabilistic, information-theoretic framework. The coexistence of local and global constraints is precisely what makes the problem difficult to address in this framework: the local rule can be enforced through vertex-level constraints, whereas the global constraint cannot be captured by independent edge probabilities. We show that this obstacle can be overcome by defining a maximum-entropy probability distribution over graphs, in which edge costs and degree constraints generate an assignment-like ensemble, and a global term, describing the hard constraint, tilts this ensemble toward Hamiltonian cycles. To make the construction tractable, we derive a mean-field approximation in terms of edge occupancies and implement a differentiable cycle penalty that suppresses sub-tours. This leads to a self-consistent numerical procedure whose output is not only a candidate tour but also a probability matrix encoding competing edges and degenerate solutions. We test the method on synthetic ensembles and on TSPLIB instances. The algorithm converges to connected tours in polynomial time, matching the best-known solution in the majority of instances and remaining within a small relative gap otherwise. Beyond its competitive performance, the proposed framework offers a general approach for handling hard constraints while reducing hard combinatorial optimization problems to simpler ones.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a probabilistic, information-theoretic framework for solving the Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP). It defines a maximum-entropy distribution over graphs where edge costs and degree constraints create an assignment-like ensemble, tilted by a global term toward Hamiltonian cycles. A mean-field approximation with a differentiable cycle penalty enables a self-consistent numerical procedure that outputs both a candidate tour and a probability matrix of competing edges. The method converges in polynomial time, matching best-known solutions on most TSPLIB instances.
AI.motivation: The TSP is hard because it couples simple local constraints (each city visited once) with a global constraint (single cycle covering all cities). The authors aim to overcome the difficulty of expressing global constraints within a probabilistic framework, since independent edge probabilities cannot capture the Hamiltonian cycle requirement.
AI.method: The method defines a maximum-entropy probability distribution over graphs. Local degree constraints generate an assignment-like ensemble, while a global term tilts the ensemble toward Hamiltonian cycles. A mean-field approximation is derived in terms of edge occupancies, and a differentiable cycle penalty is implemented to suppress sub-tours. This yields a self-consistent numerical procedure producing a candidate tour plus a probability matrix of competing edges.
AI.result: Tested on synthetic ensembles and TSPLIB instances, the algorithm converges to connected tours in polynomial time. It matches the best-known solution on the majority of instances and stays within a small relative gap otherwise.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a general approach for handling hard constraints by reducing hard combinatorial optimization problems to simpler probabilistic ones, extending beyond TSP to other combinatorial problems with similar structural challenges.

title: Hidden Frustration in Collinear Altermagnets: Pairing Vortices and Equilibrium Spin Current Loops
summary: We show that a magnet can remain perfectly collinear while its quantum vacuum circulates. In a centrosymmetric altermagnet, a symmetry-allowed locally staggered Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling imprints a gauge-irremovable vortex-antivortex pair into the anomalous magnon pair correlations at high-symmetry points in momentum space. In real space, these hidden vortices produce an antiferrochiral array of equilibrium spin currents circulating oppositely around neighboring plaquettes. Gauge-irremovable frustration therefore survives despite classical collinearity: it exists entirely in the quantum correlations. Our results show that complex pairing, gauge-invariant fluxes, and equilibrium loop currents - structures encountered across electronic flux phases, spin liquids, and frustrated quantum magnets - can be encoded in the squeezed vacuum of a collinear magnet.

AI.tldr: A centrosymmetric altermagnet can remain perfectly collinear in its classical spin order while its quantum vacuum hosts gauge-irremovable vortex-antivortex pairs in anomalous magnon pair correlations, producing antiferrochiral equilibrium spin currents that circulate oppositely around neighboring plaquettes. This demonstrates that quantum frustration can exist entirely in quantum correlations without classical magnetic order breakdown.
AI.motivation: To show that magnetic frustration and complex quantum structures (vortices, fluxes, loop currents) typically associated with non-collinear magnetic orders or frustrated quantum magnets can instead be encoded in the squeezed vacuum of a perfectly collinear magnet, via symmetry-allowed locally staggered Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling in centrosymmetric altermagnets.
AI.method: The authors analyze a centrosymmetric altermagnet in which a symmetry-allowed locally staggered Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya coupling exists. They examine anomalous magnon pair correlations at high-symmetry points in momentum space, demonstrating that this coupling imprints a gauge-irremovable vortex-antivortex pair. They then map these hidden vortices to real-space equilibrium spin currents forming an antiferrochiral array around neighboring plaquettes.
AI.result: The magnet retains perfect collinear classical order while its quantum vacuum exhibits vortices in anomalous magnon pairing, producing antiferrochiral equilibrium spin loop currents. The frustration is gauge-irremovable, meaning it cannot be eliminated by gauge transformations, yet it exists purely in the quantum correlations rather than in the classical spin configuration.
AI.conclusion: Complex pairing, gauge-invariant fluxes, and equilibrium loop currents—structures previously encountered in electronic flux phases, spin liquids, and frustrated quantum magnets—can be realized entirely within the squeezed vacuum of a collinear magnet, decoupling quantum frustration from classical magnetic non-collinearity.

title: Beyond Allen-Heine-Cardona: non-perturbative electron-phonon interactions in the linewidths and lineshifts of diamond
summary: The temperature-dependent band gap of solids is usually computed from the perturbative Allen-Heine-Cardona (AHC) electron-phonon self-energy evaluated on-shell. Extending AHC to arbitrary frequency $ω$ to determine the full spectral function via the Dyson equation is known to fail, misplacing satellites and yielding no broadening at band extrema, while non-perturbative supercell (SC) methods have focused on eigenvalue averages rather than lineshapes, and approaches based on special displacements cannot describe the full lineshape, or the lineshift at degenerate bands. Here we use a non-perturbative Green's function method (NPG), stochastically sampling distorted SC configurations, from which the spectral function, including lineshift, linewidth, and asymmetry, follows directly, and we recover finite spectral weight at the renormalized band extrema. We prove that the perturbative self-energy, computed to any order with the bare propagator and introduced into the Dyson equation, has an imaginary part that vanishes within the bare gap, giving incorrect spectral functions: self-consistency of the propagator is essential to broaden the band edges. NPG satisfies this property by construction, and contains all non-bubble diagrams. We also give a simple explanation of why SC methods converge with much smaller SCs than the corresponding $\mathbf{q}$-grids required by perturbation theory. For the band gap shift itself, the NPG and on-shell AHC results are found to be comparable, demonstrating that higher-order terms do not significantly alter the resulting renormalization in diamond. When it comes to the spectral function though, our results show that going beyond bare perturbation theory is not merely more accurate, but necessary, and NPG provides a robust framework to capture spectral broadening and higher-order effects from first principles.

AI.tldr: A non-perturbative Green's function (NPG) method is introduced to compute the full spectral function of solids from electron-phonon coupling, capturing lineshift, linewidth, and asymmetry. The authors prove that perturbative Allen-Heine-Cardona (AHC) self-energy used in the Dyson equation yields incorrect spectral functions with vanishing imaginary part within the bare gap, and that propagator self-consistency is essential. NPG reproduces comparable band gap renormalization to on-shell AHC in diamond but goes beyond to describe spectral broadening and higher-order effects from first principles.
AI.motivation: The standard perturbative AHC approach to electron-phonon coupling fails to produce correct spectral functions when extended to arbitrary frequency, misplacing satellites and yielding no broadening at band extrema. Non-perturbative supercell methods have focused only on eigenvalue averages rather than full lineshapes. A framework is needed to capture the complete spectral function including higher-order effects.
AI.method: The authors employ a non-perturbative Green's function (NPG) method that stochastically samples distorted supercell configurations. The spectral function is directly obtained from these samples, including lineshift, linewidth, and asymmetry. They prove analytically that the perturbative self-energy evaluated with the bare propagator and inserted into the Dyson equation has a vanishing imaginary part within the bare gap, demonstrating that self-consistency of the propagator is necessary. NPG satisfies self-consistency by construction and includes all non-bubble diagrams.
AI.result: NPG recovers finite spectral weight at renormalized band extrema, which perturbative approaches fail to do. The band gap shift from NPG is comparable to on-shell AHC in diamond, showing higher-order terms do not significantly alter the renormalization. However, for the spectral function itself, going beyond perturbation theory is necessary, not merely more accurate. The method also explains why supercell methods converge with much smaller supercells than the q-grids required in perturbation theory.
AI.conclusion: The NPG method provides a robust first-principles framework for capturing spectral broadening and higher-order electron-phonon effects, going beyond what bare perturbation theory can achieve. Self-consistency of the propagator is essential for broadening band edges, and NPG provides this by construction while yielding comparable band gap renormalization to established perturbative methods.

title: Influence of Many-Body Dipole-Dipole Interactions on Excitation Transfer in a Dense Gas
summary: We study non-radiative dipole-dipole induced excitation transfer in dense Rb vapour. We show that density dependence of characteristic time of the excitation diffusion changes from linear to non-linear for high Rb density. It is attributed to the breakdown of binary collisions approach to the dipole-dipole excitation transfer. It is shown that the observed result can be qualitatively described if the mean free path is replaced by mean interatomic distance for the chracteristic diffusion length.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates non-radiative dipole-dipole excitation transfer in dense rubidium vapor, finding that the characteristic time's density dependence shifts from linear to non-linear at high Rb densities, attributed to breakdown of the binary collision approximation. This is explained by replacing the mean free path with the mean interatomic distance as the characteristic diffusion length.
AI.motivation: To understand how excitation diffusion behaves in dense Rb vapour, specifically to investigate when and why the standard binary collision approach to dipole-dipole excitation transfer fails at high densities.
AI.method: Experimental study of non-radiative dipole-dipole induced excitation transfer in Rb vapour, measuring the density dependence of the characteristic excitation diffusion time across varying Rb densities and comparing observed behavior with a model where the characteristic diffusion length is taken as the mean interatomic distance rather than the mean free path.
AI.result: The characteristic time of excitation diffusion shows a linear density dependence at low Rb density but transitions to a non-linear dependence at high density. This transition signals the breakdown of the binary collision approximation. The observed behavior is qualitatively reproduced when the mean free path is replaced by the mean interatomic distance as the diffusion length scale.
AI.conclusion: In dense Rb vapour, the binary collision model fails to describe dipole-dipole excitation transfer, and a revised model using mean interatomic distance as the characteristic diffusion length qualitatively captures the observed non-linear density dependence.

title: Dynamical signatures of deconfined spinons in dimerized sawtooth chains
summary: We study the ground-state properties and dynamical response of the Heisenberg model on the sawtooth chain in and away from the exactly solvable valence-bond-solid (VBS) point. We employ U(1)-symmetric density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) and time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) methods to compute equilibrium diagnostics and the zero-temperature dynamical structure factor (DSF) $S^{zz}(q,ω)$ across the dimerized phase, a valence-bond-ordered state in which the two symmetry-equivalent apex--base bonds of each triangle develop unequal spin correlations, probing the approach to the continuous lower phase boundary, the exact VBS point, and the approach to the first-order upper boundary. In every regime, the DSF is a broad continuum dominated by a bright band at its lower edge, with the intensity at the one-triplon energy $ω\simeq J_{AB}$ suppressed. We identify the spectrum as a deconfined two-spinon continuum of kink and antikink domain walls between the two degenerate singlet coverings. Closed-form spinon dispersions fix the continuum edges and track the dominant band across the zone in all three regimes, while an explicit finite-separation two-kink calculation in a constrained Hilbert space reproduces the measured intensity distribution. Our results provide a microscopic picture of fractionalized excitations in the dimerized sawtooth chain and are relevant to the recently discovered Ti$^{3+}$ kagome fluorides, where strongly anisotropic exchange interactions can generate sawtooth-chain building blocks.

title: Low-temperature magnetism and spin dynamics in the disordered triangular-lattice Yb$^{3+}$ compound LiCaYb$_5$(BO$_3$)$_6$
summary: The interplay between geometric frustration, spin--orbit coupling, and structural disorder can give rise to unconventional magnetic ground states in rare-earth triangular-lattice magnets. Magnetic susceptibility and magnetization measurements indicate a well-isolated effective $J_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/2$ Kramers doublet with weak antiferromagnetic interactions ($θ_{\mathrm{CW}} \approx -0.54$~K). The specific heat reveals a weak anomaly near 0.43 K, suggesting the development of short-range correlated magnetism rather than conventional long-range order. $^7$Li NMR spectra broaden strongly upon cooling, consistent with increasingly inhomogeneous internal magnetic fields. The spin-lattice relaxation exhibits two relaxation components consistent with disorder-induced distributions of local magnetic environments arising from antisite disorder and competing exchange pathways. Our results establish LCYBO as a structurally disordered frustrated triangular-lattice magnet with correlated low-energy spin dynamics.

title: Strain-driven orbital-selective reconstruction and bicollinear-to-stripe evolution in FeTe
summary: FeTe, as a representative parent material among iron-based superconductors, provides an ideal platform for exploring the interplay among orbital-selective correlations, magnetism, and unconventional superconductivity. Moderate strain gives rise to a regime where more coherent quasiparticles coexist with suppressed local moments. Further strain drives FeTe into an incoherent correlated regime with robust local moments and Fe-$3d_{z^2}$-dominated low-energy states. These results establish a strain-driven trajectory across distinct magnetic and correlated electronic states in FeTe.

title: Laser-Induced Rashba Spin-Orbit Torques in Multiferroic Semiconductor (Ge,Mn)Te

summary: The multiferroic semiconductor GeMnTe exhibits ferroelectricity, strong Rashba spin-orbit coupling, and carrier-mediated magnetic order, making it a unique platform for exploring the interplay among electronic, structural, and magnetic degrees of freedom.
