The transient change in magnetic ordering, observed as variations in the coercive field, is attributed to laser-induced modifications of the ferroelectric sublattice displacement, which affect the ferroelectric polarization and the associated Rashba spin-orbit interaction. title: Diatom frustules as naturally occurring resonant microarchitectures: revealing vibrational eigenmodes across pennate and centric species
summary: Diatom frustules, the hierarchically structured, species-specific silica exoskeletons of diatom microalgae, are among Nature's most sophisticated examples of bottom-up self-assembly, exhibiting nanoscale porosity, multifunctional mechanical and optical properties, and a morphological diversity that spans nearly three orders of magnitude in size. Despite growing interest in their optical and static mechanical properties, the elastodynamic behaviour of frustules has remained largely unexplored. Here we report the first experimental detection and spatially resolved reconstruction of vibrational eigenmodes in diatom frustules, combining laser Doppler vibrometry with morphology-faithful finite-element models informed by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and focused-ion-beam scanning electron microscopy (FIB-SEM). Two morphologically contrasting taxa were investigated as model systems: the pennate diatom Rhaphoneis amphiceros and the centric diatom Stictodiscus californicus var. nitida, spanning the two principal branches of diatom diversity. Four eigenmodes were identified for R. amphiceros in the 5.90-14.17 MHz range and three for S. californicus in the 9.96-17.62 MHz range; the simulations yield a complete modal landscape for each species, including modally split and nearly degenerate eigenmodes arising from deviations from ideal symmetry, and show quantitative agreement with the experimentally measured mode shapes and resonant frequencies. These results establish diatom frustules as a class of naturally occurring resonant microarchitectures, and open new avenues for their integration as bio-derived functional elements in nanomechanical and MEMS/NEMS applications.

title: Fluctuation--response relations from an emergent $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry in the rotating stochastic Landau model
summary: In this work, we investigate the extent to which fluctuation--response relations emerge from coarse-grained stochastic dynamics alone, and which aspects instead depend on additional information about the system. To address this question, we study the rotating stochastic Landau model, an exactly solvable system describing an overdamped charged Brownian particle in a constant magnetic field, coupled dissipatively to a rotating environment, whose steady state supports circulating probability currents. Using the Martin--Siggia--Rose path integral, we show that there is an emergent $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry transformation that implements the time-reversed dynamics and changes the action by a boundary term. Comparison with the Crooks fluctuation theorem identifies this term with the entropy associated with transitions between steady-state configurations. After coupling the theory to external sources, the same symmetry yields Ward identities relating fluctuations and response. These identities follow entirely from the coarse-grained stochastic theory and do not fix the noise strength. Finally, upon imposing the Einstein relation, we show that they coincide with the high-temperature fluctuation--dissipation relations implied by the rotating Kubo--Martin--Schwinger condition for a microscopic Gibbs ensemble.

Imposing the Einstein relation, these match high-temperature fluctuation-dissipation relations from the rotating Kubo-Martin-Schwinger condition for a microscopic Gibbs ensemble.

title: How quantum is quantum geometry?
summary: The quantum geometric tensor - the Berry curvature together with the quantum metric - now underlies a long list of observables, from the anomalous Hall effect to the superfluid weight of a flat band. We ask which of these observables actually require quantum mechanics. To answer this question, we study a purely classical system: a point particle carrying a classical magnetic moment $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ that precesses in a momentum-dependent magnetic field $\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{p})$. Within Hamiltonian classical mechanics, the component of $\boldsymbol{\ell}$ along the field reproduces the Berry-curvature phenomena, while its precessing transverse component reproduces the quantum-metric phenomena. The particle acquires a position spread whose second moment is the metric, an orbital magnetic moment, and - most strikingly - an inertial mass generated by a position-dependent force, and with it a nonzero Drude weight in a system that is nominally dispersionless.

The authors question which of these observables genuinely require quantum mechanics, motivating a classical analogue to delineate the boundary between classical and quantum origins.

They analyze the resulting classical dynamics and show that the field-parallel component of the moment yields Berry-curvature phenomena, while the precessing transverse component yields quantum-metric phenomena (position spread with second moment equal to the metric, orbital magnetic moment, and an inertial mass from a position-dependent force).

Notably, it exhibits a position spread whose second moment is the metric, an orbital magnetic moment, and—most strikingly—a generated inertial mass with a nonzero Drude weight in a nominally dispersionless system.

title: Topology-Controlled Phonon Dielectric Response Beyond Density Scaling in Metal-Organic Frameworks
summary: Effective-medium theory treats material porosity as passive dilution. Using ab initio density functional theory and high-resolution synchrotron terahertz (THz) spectroscopy on isochemical zeolitic-imidazolate frameworks, we show that while the electronic permittivity obeys Clausius-Mossotti density scaling, the phonon contribution violates the conventional density scaling rules. Identical Born charges rule out the role of local chemistry. Instead, the framework connectivity localizes the THz response, where the coherency of phonon eigenvectors determines the mode-effective charges. Long-range architecture of framework topology ubiquitous in metal-organic frameworks is therefore a dielectric degree of freedom beyond the density scaling of conventional solids.

Identical Born charges rule out local chemistry; instead, framework connectivity localizes the THz response, where phonon eigenvector coherency determines mode-effective charges. Thus, long-range framework topology is a dielectric degree of freedom beyond density scaling.

Born charges are identical, excluding local chemistry effects. The violation arises from framework connectivity, which localizes the THz response and is governed by the coherency of phonon eigenvectors determining mode-effective charges.
AI.conclusion: Long-range framework architecture/topology, ubiquitous in metal-organic frameworks, acts as a dielectric degree of freedom that transcends the density-scaling behavior of conventional solids, meaning porosity cannot be treated as purely passive dilution for lattice-vibration contributions.

title: Competition between Geometrical Frustration and the Kondo Effect in CePdAl Revealed by High-Resolution Magnetization

summary: CePdAl is a heavy-fermion compound with a quasi-kagome structure, where geometrical frustration competes with the Kondo effect. Using a high-sensitivity magnetometer, we observe clear first-order metamagnetic transitions without magnetization plateaus in CePdAl at 80 mK, indicating a lifting of frustration through the suppression of the Kondo effect and spin flips of ordered moments under fields. Furthermore, we found no evidence of non-Fermi-liquid behavior in the high-field region, where the antiferromagnetic order is completely suppressed. These findings establish the essential thermodynamic constraints for understanding the field-induced spin-liquid state in CePdAl.

title: Stabilization of Interband Phase Solitons in Two-Band Noncentrosymmetric Superconducting Rings
comment: 6 pages of the main text with 4 figures and the supplemental material. Comments are welcome
summary: Two-band superconductors maintain a relative interband phase which can carry winding soliton excitations in a superconducting ring, supported by independent winding numbers in the two bands. In rings of superconductors obeying the inversion symmetry the interband phase solitons are metastable states, separated from the uniform ground state by the energy of screening currents. In this work we find that, breaking the inversion symmetry strongly enough, one can make the soliton a true ground state. In that case, a magneto-electric coupling, absent in centrosymmetric materials, contributes critically above a certain threshold, a relevant, free-energy term, odd with respect to the winding number, which biases the energy balance in favor of a particular winding sign. Once the bias outweighs the energy cost that originally made the soliton metastable, a phase soliton with a finite winding number becomes the ground state, with chirality set by the applied field. In current--flux measurements performed in equilibrium states, the effect is demonstrated by field-odd soliton branches, that replace the metastable ones existing in mesoscopic rings, built by two-component superconductors, realizing a magneto-electric analog of the Little--Parks fluxoid-branch physics in the interband relative-phase sector.

title: Above Room-Temperature Phase Transition in Helicoidal 2D Halide Perovskite Enables Pyro-Phototronic Control
summary: Bridging pyro-phototronic and ferroelectric properties in a single material not only gives rise to exotic physical phenomena but also provides strategy to build-up next-generation multi-functional energy harvesting devices. The layered halide perovskites are emerging class of synergetic 2D-materials of exceptional light-induced functionalities. Here, we report synthesis of a lead-free perovskite (3-fluorobenzylamine)2CuCl4 of partially fluorinated aromatic rings. Molecular chains are chiral in helicoids so to render flexibility, energy-transfer, and freedom to tailor tunable pyro-phototronics on light illumination. The fluorinated framework promotes ferroelectric-to-paraelectric transition point (TC), as high as \textasciitilde 412 K of wide range of workably. A giant pyro-photronic response is distinctly evident even upon UV-visible light-illuminations. A significantly high pyro-photronic current of 60 nA was achieved under an illumination of λex\textasciitilde 365 nm (27 mW) in a self-powered configuration. Consequently, an intricate coupling of the spontaneous polarization to the optical properties is visualized from the piezo response force microscopy (PFM) responses. In particular, the polar domains get diminished reversibly in on-off steps of the light irradiations. It indicates, the light provides another degree of the freedom to control the features for the applications of optoelectronic devices, optical memories, photo/thermo-chromic systems, and energy-harvesters.

PFM studies reveal reversible light-controlled polar domain modulation, demonstrating coupled ferroelectric and photonic functionalities for optoelectronic, memory, chromic, and energy-harvesting applications.

title: Diamond quantum-sensing platform with integrated boron-doped diamond microwave antenna and thermometer
summary: Wide-field nitrogen-vacancy (NV) magnetic imaging at cryogenic temperatures requires microwave excitation and reliable knowledge of the temperature near the sensing region. The BDD antenna provides microwave excitation for optically detected magnetic resonance measurements, and the BDD thermometer monitors the thermal environment near the NV sensing region. The BDD thermometer detected laser-induced local heating that was not clearly resolved by a stage-mounted thermometer. Using this platform, we imaged the temperature-dependent Meissner response of multiple cuprate superconductors while recording the temperature. These results demonstrate that the integrated BDD--NV platform provides a practical approach for cryogenic wide-field magnetic imaging with integrated microwave delivery and local thermometry.

title: When dissipative steady states admit thermodynamic occupation laws
summary: Non-equilibrium steady states (NESSs) generally lack thermodynamic occupation laws because finite stationary circulation and a globally exact rate-ratio field cannot coexist for the same Markov generator. Here we construct a sector-separated geometry that overcomes this incompatibility without arresting dissipation. Entropy-production exposure-and-separation excludes the entropy-producing state~$0$ from the conditional occupation manifold while retaining it in the dissipative full graph; physical returns $i\to0\to0^\ast$ become effectively Markovian in the strong-bias/rapid-reset (SR) limit. For a thermodynamically complete conditional manifold, autonomous redistribution (AR) eliminates residual futile circulation, making the rate-ratio one-form exact. Thermodynamic calibration gives $X_i=β(Δμ- \mathcal F_i^{\mathrm{cost}})$ and $p_i=e^{X_i}/Z_\mathcal{C}$, with $Z_\mathcal{C}=1+\sum_i e^{X_i}$. Full-graph probabilities factorize exactly as $P_α=(1-P_0)p_α$. In the SR limit, the kinetic factor tends to unity while $p_α\to e^{X_α}/Z_\mathcal C$, yielding $P_α\to p_α$ while finite dissipation persists. Near AR, integrability is lost linearly in residual cycle current whereas dissipation begins quadratically. In the binary zero-cycle-rank limit, occupation redistributes autonomously under maintained $Δμ$ bias, yielding the inverted Fermi--Dirac law, which is applied to thermal smearing in quantum-dot lasers. The framework provides constructive acquisition conditions and failure diagnostics for thermodynamic occupation laws in dissipative NESSs.

AI.tldr: This paper constructs a sector-separated geometry that enables thermodynamic occupation laws to coexist with finite stationary circulation in non-equilibrium steady states (NESSs). It uses entropy-production exposure-and-separation to exclude the entropy-producing state from the conditional occupation manifold, employs autonomous redistribution (AR) to eliminate residual futile circulation, and derives exact Boltzmann-like occupation laws $p_i = e^{X_i}/Z_\mathcal{C}$ with thermodynamic calibration $X_i = \beta(\Delta\mu - \mathcal{F}_i^\text{cost})$. In the strong-bias/rapid-reset limit, full-graph probabilities converge to the conditional ones while dissipation persists. Near AR, integrability is lost linearly in residual cycle current while dissipation scales quadratically. In the binary zero-cycle-rank limit, the framework yields an inverted Fermi–Dirac law, applied to thermal smearing in quantum-dot lasers.

The authors seek to overcome this fundamental incompatibility—without arresting dissipation—by constructing a geometrical framework that allows for exact occupation laws in dissipative NESSs, thereby extending equilibrium thermodynamics to far-from-equilibrium conditions.
AI.method: The method introduces a sector-separated geometry based on entropy-production exposure-and-separation: the entropy-producing state 0 is excluded from the conditional occupation manifold while retained in the dissipative full graph, making physical returns $i \to 0 \to 0^\ast$ effectively Markovian in the strong-bias/rapid-reset (SR) limit. A thermodynamically complete conditional manifold is achieved via autonomous redistribution (AR), which eliminates residual futile circulation, rendering the rate-ratio one-form exact. Thermodynamic calibration then yields $X_i = \beta(\Delta\mu - \mathcal{F}_i^\text{cost})$ and $p_i = e^{X_i}/Z_\mathcal{C}$ with $Z_\mathcal{C} = 1 + \sum_i e^{X_i}$, and full-graph probabilities factorize exactly as $P_\alpha = (1-P_0) p_\alpha$.
AI.result: In the SR limit, the kinetic factor tends to unity while $p_\alpha \to e^{X_\alpha}/Z_\mathcal{C}$, giving $P_\alpha \to p_\alpha$ while finite dissipation remains. Near AR, integrability is lost linearly in residual cycle current whereas dissipation begins quadratically. In the binary zero-cycle-rank limit, occupation redistributes autonomously under maintained $\Delta\mu$ bias, producing an inverted Fermi–Dirac law, which is applied to thermal smearing in quantum-dot lasers. The framework also provides constructive acquisition conditions and failure diagnostics for thermodynamic occupation laws in dissipative NESSs.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that thermodynamic occupation laws are attainable in dissipative non-equilibrium steady states through a carefully constructed sector-separated geometry, without requiring dissipation arrest. The derived exact occupation statistics, including the inverted Fermi–Dirac law in specific limits, provide a constructive and diagnostic framework for extending equilibrium-style thermodynamic descriptions to NESSs, with practical application to quantum-dot lasers and broader dissipative systems.

title: Majorana signatures in an asymmetrically coupled quantum dot--topological superconducting nanowire junction
summary: We present a theoretical study of the quantum transport through a nanoscale system in which a central quantum dot (QD) is coupled asymmetrically to normal leads and to two Majorana bound states (MBSs) localized at the ends of a topological superconducting nanowire threaded by a tunable magnetic flux. The effects of the leads--QD coupling asymmetry parameter $α$ and the bias voltage asymmetry parameter $q$ on the system's linear conductance are considered for the case of unhybridized and hybridized MBSs. In the zero-temperature limit, for unhybridized MBSs the system's linear conductance is finite only when the magnetic flux phase $φ= (2n+1)π$ ($n\in\mathbb{Z}$) and it scales as $\mathcal{G}=2qαe^2/[h(α+1)]$, while for hybridized MBSs it presents a complicated dependence on the system's parameters. At finite temperature, for unhybridized MBSs, the system's linear conductance oscillates as a function of the magnetic flux phase $φ$ with a period of $2π$, and the position of the linear conductance maxima can be shifted from $φ=2nπ$ to $φ=(2n+1)π$ by simply varying the value of the bias voltage asymmetry parameter $q$. For hybridized MBSs, the conductance exhibits a similar behavior when the energy level of the central QD, $\varepsilon_d$, is tuned at the leads' Fermi level ($\varepsilon_d=\varepsilon_F$), although when $\varepsilon_d\neq\varepsilon_F$ the oscillation period changes to $4π$, and the position of the linear conductance maxima depends on the actual value of $\varepsilon_d$ and other parameters in the system. Our results highlight the experimental importance of the leads-QD and bias voltage asymmetry parameters, which are often present in realistic experimental setups, and can strongly affect the identification and observation of MBSs transport signatures.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically studies quantum transport through a quantum dot asymmetrically coupled to normal leads and two Majorana bound states (MBSs) at the ends of a topological superconducting nanowire under tunable magnetic flux. It analyzes how leads-QD coupling asymmetry (α) and bias voltage asymmetry (q) affect linear conductance for both unhybridized and hybridized MBSs at zero and finite temperature, showing that MBS conductance signatures depend sensitively on these asymmetry parameters and can be shifted by tuning them.
AI.motivation: Understanding the transport signatures of Majorana bound states is crucial for topological quantum computing, but realistic experiments always feature asymmetric lead-QD couplings and bias voltages. These asymmetries are often neglected in idealized models but can significantly distort or obscure MBS signatures, making it essential to study their effects systematically.
AI.method: The authors perform a theoretical (analytic) study of quantum transport through a central quantum dot coupled asymmetrically to normal leads and to two MBSs at the nanowire ends, with a tunable magnetic flux phase φ. They consider the linear conductance in the zero-temperature limit and at finite temperature, separately for unhybridized and hybridized MBS cases, and examine the roles of the coupling asymmetry parameter α and the bias voltage asymmetry parameter q.
AI.result: At zero temperature with unhybridized MBSs, conductance is finite only when φ=(2n+1)π and scales as G=2qαe²/[h(α+1)]. At finite temperature, conductance oscillates with period 2π in φ, and the conductance maxima position can be tuned from φ=2nπ to φ=(2n+1)π by changing q. For hybridized MBSs, similar behavior occurs when εd=εF, but when εd≠εF the oscillation period changes to 4π and the maxima positions depend on εd and other parameters.
AI.conclusion: The leads-QD coupling asymmetry and bias voltage asymmetry parameters, often present in realistic experiments, strongly affect MBS transport signatures and can shift or reshape them. This has important experimental implications for correctly identifying and observing Majorana bound states in topological superconducting systems.

title: Field-amplified readouts of weak altermagnetic exchange in MnF$_2$
summary: MnF$_2$, the textbook two-sublattice antiferromagnet, has reemerged as a prototypical altermagnet, yet the sublattice-odd exchange that defines this identity remains under active debate: it enters the magnon splitting only in quadrature with the dipole--dipole interaction, its magnitude suppressed and its sign erased. An overdetermined first-principles total-energy mapping resolves this scale as a seventh-neighbor imbalance $δ{J_7}\simeq+8~μ$eV. The resulting Hamiltonian, with the dipole--dipole interaction included explicitly, reproduces the low-energy gap and the visible finite-momentum splitting. A longitudinal field $B\parallel c$ then acts as a linear amplifier of the hidden scale, opening two signed, field-linear readouts. The first is the compensation field $B^\ast(\mathbf Q)$, the position of minimum splitting, which is equal and opposite at the rotation-related partner momenta: a shift from zero field is itself evidence of a finite imbalance, its side gives the sign, and its magnitude, $|B^\ast|\simeq0.34$~T here, gives the scale. The second is the fixed-field contrast of the partner splittings, $\simeq0.14$~meV at $1$~T, six times the zero-field excess: a sign check from just two spectra. Both readouts survive a $0.12$~meV energy resolution, and the construction carries over to any easy-axis collinear altermagnet, bringing $μ$eV altermagnetic exchange within present instrumental reach.

AI.tldr: The paper resolves the debated sublattice-odd exchange in MnF2 (a prototypical altermagnet) via overdetermined first-principles total-energy mapping, finding a small seventh-neighbor imbalance δJ7 ≈ +8 μeV. Including dipole–dipole interactions, the Hamiltonian reproduces the low-energy gap and finite-momentum splitting. A longitudinal field B∥c acts as a linear amplifier of this hidden scale, enabling two signed, field-linear readouts: the compensation field B*(Q) (≈0.34 T) and fixed-field partner-splitting contrast (≈0.14 meV at 1 T, six times the zero-field excess), both robust at 0.12 meV resolution and generalizable to any easy-axis collinear altermagnet.
AI.motivation: The sublattice-odd exchange defining MnF2's altermagnetic identity is experimentally elusive because it enters magnon splitting only in quadrature with the dipole–dipole interaction, which suppresses its magnitude and erases its sign. An unambiguous determination of this scale is needed.
AI.method: An overdetermined first-principles total-energy mapping extracts the sublattice-odd exchange as a seventh-neighbor imbalance (δJ7 ≈ +8 μeV). The resulting Hamiltonian includes the dipole–dipole interaction explicitly and reproduces the low-energy gap and finite-momentum splitting. The framework then applies a longitudinal field B∥c as a linear amplifier, yielding two field-linear observables: the compensation field B*(Q) marking minimum splitting at rotation-related partner momenta, and the fixed-field contrast between partner splittings.
AI.result: The compensation field magnitude is ≈0.34 T, its side reveals the sign of the imbalance. The fixed-field partner-splitting contrast is ≈0.14 meV at 1 T—six times the zero-field excess. Both readouts survive a 0.12 meV energy resolution.
AI.conclusion: Longitudinal-field magnon measurements bring μeV-scale altermagnetic exchange within present instrumental reach, and the construction generalizes to any easy-axis collinear altermagnet.

title: High-Temperature Superconductivity of the Fe-Se-H compound
summary: Using an EPR spectrometer, the dependences of microwave power absorption on magnetic field up to 6000 Oe were measured at temperatures of 3.6-25 K and 295 K in a powdered compound Fe-Se-H, obtained by thermal diffusion of hydrogen into a FeSe single crystal with a critical temperature of 8 K. The shape of the dependences and the analysis of the measurement results confirm the superconductivity of the Fe-Se-H compound at normal pressure, both at temperatures of 3.6-25 K and at 295 K, i.e., at room temperature.

AI.tldr: The paper reports EPR spectrometer measurements of microwave power absorption as a function of magnetic field (up to 6000 Oe) in a powdered Fe-Se-H compound (hydrogenated FeSe) at temperatures from 3.6 K to 295 K. The results indicate the compound exhibits superconductivity at normal pressure not only at low temperatures (3.6-25 K) but also at room temperature (295 K).
AI.motivation: To investigate whether hydrogenated FeSe (Fe-Se-H) exhibits superconductivity at room temperature under normal pressure, which would be a major breakthrough in superconductivity research.
AI.method: EPR (Electron Paramagnetic Resonance) spectrometer measurements of microwave power absorption dependence on magnetic field up to 6000 Oe, performed on a powdered Fe-Se-H sample (prepared by thermal diffusion of hydrogen into an FeSe single crystal with Tc=8 K) across temperatures of 3.6-25 K and 295 K.
AI.result: The shape of the microwave power absorption vs. magnetic field dependences and subsequent analysis confirm superconductivity in Fe-Se-H at normal pressure at both low temperatures (3.6-25 K) and at room temperature (295 K).
AI.conclusion: Fe-Se-H exhibits superconductivity at normal pressure even at room temperature, suggesting that hydrogenated FeSe may be a promising candidate for room-temperature superconductors under ambient conditions.

title: Magnetic permeability and zone-folded phonons in layered NiPS$_3$
summary: Nickel phosphorus trisulfide (NiPS$_3$) stands out as a Mott insulator exhibiting XY-type antiferromagnetic order. In this work, we investigate the electrodynamic response of single-crystalline NiPS$_3$ using Terahertz Time-Domain Spectroscopy (THz-TDS) as a function of temperature. In cases where the magnetic permeability cannot be approximated to unity, conventional THz transmission analysis is often restricted to the complex refractive index, hindering the distinction between magnetic and dielectric contributions. To overcome this limitation, we demonstrate an extraction methodology capable of decoupling the magnetic permeability from the electric permittivity. Assuming that the dielectric contribution remains invariant below the N'eel temperature (TN), we used data from the paramagnetic phase to isolate the intrinsic magnetic component at 13 K. The angular and thermal dependence of the spectra revealed a magnon mode near 1 THz (for 0$^\circ$ orientation) and, distinctively, a zone-folded phonon activated by symmetry breaking (at 90$^\circ$). The isolated magnetic permeability was successfully modeled using Drude-Lorentz oscillators, enabling the extraction of fundamental spin dynamics parameters in this material.

AI.tldr: This work develops a THz-TDS methodology to decouple magnetic permeability from electric permittivity in NiPS3, a Mott insulator with XY-type antiferromagnetic order, isolating a magnon mode near 1 THz and a zone-folded phonon, and modeling the magnetic response with Drude-Lorentz oscillators to extract spin dynamics parameters.
AI.motivation: Conventional THz transmission analysis in materials where magnetic permeability cannot be approximated to unity is limited to extracting only the complex refractive index, which makes it impossible to distinguish between magnetic and dielectric contributions. A methodology is needed to isolate these contributions to study the intrinsic spin dynamics in NiPS3.
AI.method: Terahertz Time-Domain Spectroscopy (THz-TDS) measurements on single-crystalline NiPS3 as a function of temperature. An extraction methodology is developed to decouple magnetic permeability from electric permittivity by assuming the dielectric contribution is invariant below the Néel temperature, using paramagnetic-phase data to isolate the intrinsic magnetic component at 13 K. The isolated magnetic permeability is modeled using Drude-Lorentz oscillators, with angular and thermal dependence of spectra analyzed at 0° and 90° orientations.
AI.result: A magnon mode near 1 THz was identified at 0° orientation, and a zone-folded phonon activated by symmetry breaking was found at 90°. The isolated magnetic permeability was successfully modeled using Drude-Lorentz oscillators, enabling extraction of fundamental spin dynamics parameters.
AI.conclusion: The developed methodology successfully decouples magnetic and dielectric contributions in NiPS3, allowing for the extraction of intrinsic magnetic response and key spin dynamics parameters in this antiferromagnetic Mott insulator.

title: Hyperuniformity as a unifying organizational principle across diatom architectures
summary: Diatom frustules have long fascinated scientists for the extraordinary beauty, diversity, and functionality of their intricate silica architectures. Yet, the spatial organization of these structures has so far been primarily described in terms of morphology, symmetry, and crystallographic order, leaving common statistical properties across distinct diatom architectures largely unexplored. By analyzing diatom frustules through the lens of hyperuniformity for the first time, we reveal a striking commonality across their remarkable diversity: all analyzed genera exhibit signatures of suppressed long-wavelength density fluctuations. Specifically, we find that these architectures range from strongly ordered Class I to disordered Class III hyperuniform systems. We show that local order, spatial correlations, and long-range fluctuation suppression can vary partially independently, giving rise to a continuous spectrum of multiscale architectures. Our multiscale approach reveals that hyperuniformity can be reliably characterized in finite biological structures, beyond what conventional asymptotic diagnostics can resolve. Together, these results prove that hyperuniformity provides a unifying statistical framework for describing diatom diversity beyond conventional classifications of structural order.

AI.tldr: This paper applies the concept of hyperuniformity—suppressed long-wavelength density fluctuations—to analyze diatom frustules for the first time, revealing that all examined genera exhibit hyperuniform signatures ranging from ordered Class I to disordered Class III systems. This provides a unifying statistical framework for describing diatom diversity beyond traditional morphological and crystallographic classifications.
AI.motivation: While diatom frustules are celebrated for their beautiful and diverse silica architectures, their spatial organization has been primarily analyzed through morphology, symmetry, and crystallographic order. Common statistical properties shared across distinct diatom architectures remain largely unexplored, motivating the search for a unifying quantitative framework.
AI.method: The authors analyze diatom frustules through the lens of hyperuniformity, a statistical concept describing suppressed long-wavelength density fluctuations. They employ a multiscale approach that allows reliable characterization of hyperuniformity in finite biological structures, examining local order, spatial correlations, and long-range fluctuation suppression across multiple diatom genera.
AI.result: All analyzed diatom genera exhibit signatures of suppressed long-wavelength density fluctuations, ranging from strongly ordered Class I to disordered Class III hyperuniform systems. The study shows that local order, spatial correlations, and long-range fluctuation suppression can vary partially independently, producing a continuous spectrum of multiscale architectures. The multiscale method successfully characterized hyperuniformity beyond what conventional asymptotic diagnostics can resolve.
AI.conclusion: Hyperuniformity provides a unifying statistical framework for describing diatom diversity beyond conventional classifications of structural order, demonstrating that diverse diatom architectures share statistically similar long-wavelength fluctuation suppression despite their morphological differences.

title: Brownian yet non-Gaussian diffusion through equilibrium nonlinear friction
summary: In Brownian yet non-Gaussian diffusion (BnGD) the mean squared displacement grows linearly in time. However, the displacement statistics do not follow a normal distribution throughout. Typically, they are non-Gaussian at intermediate times, before they cross over to Gaussian in the long-time regime. We demonstrate that nonlinear friction under correctly applied stochastic equilibrium conditions provides an explanation of this phenomenon also for homogeneous environments.

AI.tldr: This paper explains Brownian yet non-Gaussian diffusion (BnGD) in homogeneous environments by showing that nonlinear friction, when combined with properly applied stochastic equilibrium conditions, can produce the characteristic linear mean squared displacement with non-Gaussian displacement statistics at intermediate times that eventually cross over to Gaussian behavior in the long-time limit.
AI.motivation: Brownian yet non-Gaussian diffusion (BnGD) is a phenomenon where the mean squared displacement grows linearly in time, yet the displacement statistics deviate from a normal distribution at intermediate times before becoming Gaussian at long times. The authors aim to provide an explanation for this phenomenon in homogeneous environments, which previous theoretical frameworks struggled to account for within a single mechanism.
AI.method: The authors incorporate nonlinear friction into a stochastic framework subject to correctly applied stochastic equilibrium conditions. By ensuring that the equilibrium conditions are properly imposed within the nonlinear friction model, they demonstrate that this single mechanism can reproduce the BnGD phenomenon without requiring environmental heterogeneity or superposition of multiple diffusion processes.
AI.result: The study demonstrates that nonlinear friction, under correctly applied stochastic equilibrium conditions, can explain Brownian yet non-Gaussian diffusion in homogeneous environments. The model reproduces the key features of BnGD: linear mean squared displacement, non-Gaussian displacement statistics at intermediate times, and a crossover to Gaussian statistics in the long-time regime.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that nonlinear friction combined with correct stochastic equilibrium conditions offers a unified explanation for Brownian yet non-Gaussian diffusion, even in homogeneous environments where no spatial heterogeneity or multi-component diffusion is present.

title: Magnetic Communication with an Acoustically Actuated Magnetoelectric Resonator and a Quantum Diamond Magnetometer
summary: Wireless communication via propagating magnetic fields is a communication modality that has recently garnered significant interest for short-to-medium range communication in conductive mediums, such as underwater and underground, where existing approaches utilizing electric fields are highly inefficient. Typical implementations of magnetic communication make use of loop antennas as both the transmitter and receiver, with the sensitivity and frequency response scaling with and inversely with the loop cross-sectional area, respectively. Here, we explore an alternative hybrid magnetic communication system consisting of an highly radiation efficient and compact acoustically actuated magnetoelectric resonator as the transmitter, and a highly sensitive micrometer scale quantum magnetometer based on nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond as the receiver, with their core properties unconstrained by size. We demonstrate amplitude and phase-encoded transmission and reception of AC magnetic fields at $f_{\mathrm{AC}}$ = 20 kHz, achieving a sensitivity of 50 pT/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$ and 1.2 mrad/$\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}$, respectively. This work establishes the use of hybrid magnetoelectric resonator and quantum diamond magnetometer communication system as a viable alternative to existing loop-based approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a hybrid wireless magnetic communication system using an acoustically actuated magnetoelectric resonator as transmitter and a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center diamond quantum magnetometer as receiver, achieving 20 kHz AC magnetic field communication with 50 pT/√Hz amplitude sensitivity and 1.2 mrad/√Hz phase sensitivity, demonstrating a viable alternative to conventional loop-antenna-based magnetic communication.
AI.motivation: Magnetic field-based wireless communication is attractive for conductive media (underwater, underground) where electric-field-based approaches are inefficient. However, conventional loop antennas have performance fundamentally constrained by cross-sectional area—sensitivity scales with area while frequency response inversely scales with it. This work seeks to overcome these size-related limitations by exploring a hybrid system with components whose core properties are not size-constrained.
AI.method: The authors construct a hybrid magnetic communication link comprising: (1) a compact, radiation-efficient acoustically actuated magnetoelectric resonator as the transmitter, and (2) a highly sensitive micrometer-scale quantum magnetometer based on nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond as the receiver. They demonstrate both amplitude and phase-encoded transmission and reception of AC magnetic fields at 20 kHz frequency.
AI.result: The system achieved amplitude sensitivity of 50 pT/√Hz and phase sensitivity of 1.2 mrad/√Hz at f_AC = 20 kHz, successfully demonstrating both amplitude- and phase-encoded signal transmission and reception.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid magnetoelectric resonator plus quantum diamond magnetometer communication system is established as a viable and practical alternative to existing loop-antenna-based magnetic communication approaches, offering scalable performance decoupled from component size constraints.

title: Benchmarking of Fast and Interpretable UF Machine Learning Potentials
summary: Machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have emerged as a powerful alternative to density functional theory (DFT) for molecular dynamics simulations, offering near-DFT accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. However, many state-of-the-art MLIPs remain computationally demanding and act as black boxes, limiting physical interpretability. In this work, we evaluate the ultra-fast force field (UF$^3$) potential, which employs linear regression with cubic B-spline basis to represent effective two- and three-body interactions. We show that UF$^3$ displays accuracy comparable to established models such as GAP, MTP, NNP (Behler Parrinello), and qSNAP MLIPs. We further investigate the transferability of UF$^3$ by computing melting points for six elemental systems with potentials fitted without any solid-liquid interface configurations or explicit thermodynamic information about melting. The model reproduces experimental melting points within $\sim$6% for simple metals (Ni, Cu, Li), but substantially underestimates them for Mo and Si and fails to yield a stable potential for Ge, reflecting the limitations of a fixed expansion truncated at the three-body term for systems with strong angular or covalent bonding. We further illustrate how UF$^3$'s spline-based formulation allows direct visualization of the learned interactions, enabling identification of unphysical behavior that black-box approaches often obscure.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates the ultra-fast force field (UF³) potential, a linear regression model with cubic B-spline basis for two- and three-body interactions, showing it achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art MLIPs (GAP, MTP, NNP, qSNAP) while offering physical interpretability. UF³ reproduces experimental melting points within ~6% for simple metals (Ni, Cu, Li) but underestimates them for covalent systems (Mo, Si) and fails for Ge due to truncation at three-body terms. The spline-based formulation enables direct visualization of learned interactions.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art MLIPs are computationally demanding and act as black boxes, limiting physical interpretability. There is a need for fast, interpretable interatomic potentials that maintain near-DFT accuracy.
AI.method: UF³ uses linear regression with cubic B-spline basis functions to represent effective two- and three-body interactions. Accuracy is benchmarked against GAP, MTP, NNP (Behler-Parrinello), and qSNAP. Transferability is tested by computing melting points of six elemental systems using potentials fitted without solid-liquid interface configurations or thermodynamic melting information.
AI.result: UF³ achieves accuracy comparable to established MLIPs. It reproduces experimental melting points within ~6% for simple metals (Ni, Cu, Li) but substantially underestimates Mo and Si, and fails to produce a stable potential for Ge—reflecting limitations of truncating the expansion at three-body terms for systems with strong angular/covalent bonding. The spline formulation enables direct visualization of learned interactions, revealing unphysical behavior.
AI.conclusion: UF³ offers a compelling combination of accuracy, speed, and interpretability for simple metallic systems, but its fixed truncation at three-body terms limits its applicability to strongly angular or covalently bonded materials.

title: Thermally quenched metastability in metal-insulator transitions via elemental substitution
summary: Thermal quenching inhibits equilibration toward the thermodynamic ground state during phase transitions, revealing metastable phases such as structural glasses and quenched alloys. Whether such thermally quenched metastability can be realized in metal-insulator transitions has remained an open question because these transformations are governed by collective electronic reorganization rather than atomic diffusion. We demonstrate that rapid cooling exceeding 10$^9$ K s$^{-1}$ kinetically avoids the metal-insulator transition, stabilizing a long-lived metastable metallic phase in tungsten-substituted VO$_2$. Temperature-dependent relaxation reveals nucleation-dominated kinetics with a thermal activation barrier introduced by tungsten substitution. Our results establish elemental substitution as a route to thermally quenched metastability in metal-insulator transitions, expanding metastable phase control to electronic phases.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that rapid cooling exceeding 10^9 K/s can kinetically bypass the metal-insulator transition in tungsten-substituted VO2, stabilizing a long-lived metastable metallic phase. Elemental substitution introduces a thermal activation barrier that enables nucleation-dominated relaxation kinetics, establishing a route to thermally quenched metastability in electronic phase transitions.
AI.motivation: Thermal quenching has long been used to stabilize metastable phases (e.g., structural glasses, quenched alloys) in atomic-diffusion-driven transitions, but whether such quenching metastability can be achieved in metal-insulator transitions governed by collective electronic reorganization remains an open question.
AI.method: The authors apply ultra-fast cooling (exceeding 10^9 K/s) to tungsten-substituted VO2, combined with temperature-dependent relaxation measurements to characterize the kinetics and activation barriers of the suppressed metal-insulator transition.
AI.result: Rapid cooling kinetically avoids the metal-insulator transition, stabilizing a long-lived metastable metallic phase. Relaxation studies show nucleation-dominated kinetics with a thermal activation barrier introduced by tungsten substitution.
AI.conclusion: Elemental substitution offers a viable route to thermally quenched metastability in metal-insulator transitions, expanding metastable phase control from atomic to electronic degrees of freedom.

title: The Effect of Geometry on Thermodynamic Response
summary: At the nano- and microscale, various patterns influence and shape thermal and optical response, making them essential for the survival of various biological species. In addition, controlling thermal radiation is vital for a broad range of applications, such as thermal management, spectroscopy, optoelectronics, and energy conversion technologies. For this reason, there is strong pressure to elucidate the physics of thermal radiation at the nanoscale. In this article, we provide evidence that complex nanoscale geometries affect thermal management, leading to an unusual thermal response in heat-capacity measurements as a function of temperature. Beyond identifying the structural constraints associated with this unusual thermodynamic response, the current study introduces the possibility of shaping the apparent heat-capacity response through geometry without necessarily altering the system's chemistry.

AI.tldr: This paper demonstrates that nanoscale geometric patterns can influence thermal management and produce unusual heat-capacity responses as a function of temperature, independent of chemical composition.
AI.motivation: Understanding and controlling thermal radiation at the nanoscale is vital for applications in thermal management, spectroscopy, optoelectronics, and energy conversion. There is strong pressure to elucidate nanoscale thermal radiation physics, and nanoscale patterns are known to shape thermal and optical responses crucial for biological species' survival.
AI.method: The study investigates complex nanoscale geometries and their effect on thermal management, examining heat-capacity measurements as a function of temperature, while identifying structural constraints associated with the observed unusual thermodynamic response.
AI.result: Evidence shows that complex nanoscale geometries produce an unusual thermal response in heat-capacity measurements as a function of temperature. The structural constraints linked to this response were identified, demonstrating that geometry can shape apparent heat-capacity response without altering system chemistry.
AI.conclusion: Nanoscale geometry alone can be used to engineer apparent heat-capacity responses, offering a pathway to control thermal properties without changing the chemical composition of the system.

title: Quenched activity induces nonuniversal scaling in nonreciprocal XY Models and surfaces
summary: Active XY models and active surfaces are two paradigmatic nonequilibrium systems with distinct microscopic origins. We show that the hydrodynamic theories for a quenched-disordered nonreciprocal random bond two-dimensional XY model and an inversion-symmetric active surface tangentially advected by quenched velocities are identical. This theory predicts sub-logarithmic phase order in the XY model and sub- or super-logarithmic positional order in the surface for short-range disorder with nonuniversal exponents, which vary continuously with the degree of transversality of the disorder variance. We argue that the nonreciprocal random bond XY model can disorder through vortex proliferation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that a nonreciprocal random bond XY model in 2D and an active surface advected by quenched tangential velocities share identical hydrodynamic theories, predicting sub-logarithmic order with nonuniversal exponents for short-range disorder, and suggesting vortex-proliferation-induced disordering in the XY model.
AI.motivation: To bridge two seemingly distinct nonequilibrium systems—active XY models and active surfaces—by revealing their shared hydrodynamic description, and to understand ordering behavior in the presence of quenched disorder.
AI.method: Derivation of hydrodynamic theories for a quenched-disordered nonreciprocal random bond 2D XY model and an inversion-symmetric active surface tangentially advected by quenched velocities, showing their equivalence and analyzing scaling of phase/positional order.
AI.result: The theories are identical, predicting sub-logarithmic phase order in the XY model and sub- or super-logarithmic positional order in the surface for short-range disorder, with exponents varying continuously with the transversality of the disorder variance. The nonreciprocal random bond XY model is argued to disorder via vortex proliferation.
AI.conclusion: Active XY models and active surfaces share a common hydrodynamic framework under quenched disorder, exhibiting anomalous (nonuniversal) ordering behavior and a vortex-driven disordering mechanism.

title: Statistical Disorder in MBE-Grown AlGaAs/GaAs Superlattices for Quantum Bragg Mirrors using Synchrotron X-ray Diffraction
summary: AlGaAs/GaAs superlattices grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy (MBE) are foundational for advanced optoelectronic devices, including Quantum Bragg Mirror (QBM) infrared detectors. The performance of these devices critically depends on achieving near-perfect periodicity and abrupt interfaces, however, intrinsic statistical fluctuations during MBE growth introduce nanoscale structural disorder that can degrade device efficiency. In this study, we present a comprehensive methodology for quantifying this disorder in a 203-layer QBM device. High-resolution structural characterization was performed using high-energy (25 keV) synchrotron X-ray diffraction. By coupling a recursive dynamical diffraction formalism with an ensemble simulated annealing refinement, we extracted statistically robust, layer-by-layer thickness profiles. Our analysis reveals highly systematic, material-specific deviations from the nominal design: all AlGaAs barrier layers were consistently thinner than nominal by 0.3-0.6 nm. Furthermore, the sequential thickness profile successfully identified a significant 35 nm deficit in the final macroscopic top contact layer and a 40 nm deficit in the first GaAs layer. Achieving a statistical precision of about 0.2 to 0.6 nm (approximately 1-2 atomic monolayers), this non-destructive diagnostic approach provides directly actionable feedback for MBE flux calibration protocols.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a methodology for quantifying nanoscale structural disorder in a 203-layer AlGaAs/GaAs Quantum Bragg Mirror (QBM) infrared detector grown by MBE. Using high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction combined with recursive dynamical diffraction modeling and simulated annealing refinement, the authors extracted layer-by-layer thickness profiles with statistical precision of 0.2-0.6 nm (1-2 atomic monolayers), revealing systematic material-specific deviations including 0.3-0.6 nm thinner AlGaAs barriers, a 35 nm deficit in the top contact layer, and a 40 nm deficit in the first GaAs layer.
AI.motivation: The performance of QBM infrared detectors critically depends on near-perfect periodicity and abrupt interfaces in AlGaAs/GaAs superlattices, yet intrinsic statistical fluctuations during MBE growth introduce nanoscale structural disorder that degrades device efficiency. A comprehensive, non-destructive methodology is needed to quantify this disorder and provide actionable feedback for growth calibration.
AI.method: High-resolution structural characterization was performed using high-energy (25 keV) synchrotron X-ray diffraction. A recursive dynamical diffraction formalism was coupled with an ensemble simulated annealing refinement to extract statistically robust, layer-by-layer thickness profiles from the 203-layer QBM device.
